<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">πολὺς ἄργυρός ἐστι</l> <l>καὶ χρυσὸς καὶ γῆς πυροφόρου πεδία</l> <l>ἵπποι θʼ ἡμίονοί τε, καὶ ᾧ μόνα ταῦτα πάρεστι,</l> <l>γαστρί τε καὶ πλευρῇ καὶ ποσὶν ἁβρὰ παθεῖν,</l> <l>παιδός τʼ ἠδὲ γυναικός, ἐπὴν καὶ ταῦτʼ ἀφίκηται,</l> <l>ἥβη, σὺν δʼ ὥρη γίνεται ἁρμοδία.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 24. 1-6 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">χρήματα δʼ ἱμείρω μὲν ἔχειν, ἀδίκως δὲ πεπᾶσθαι</l> <l>οὐκ ἐθέλω· πάντως ὕστερον ἦλθε δίκη.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 13. 7-8 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>κωλύει δὲ οὐδὲν τὸν ἀγαθὸν καὶ πολιτικὸν ἄνδρα μήτε τῶν περιττῶν τὴν κτῆσιν ἐν σπουδῇ τίθεσθαι μήτε τῆς χρείας τῶν ἀναγκαίων καὶ ἱκανῶν καταφρονεῖν. ἐν δὲ τοῖς τότε χρόνοις, καθʼ Ἡσίοδον, ἔργον οὐδὲν ἦν ὄνειδος, οὐδὲ τέχνη διαφορὰν ἔφερεν, ἐμπορία δὲ καὶ δόξαν εἶχεν οἰκειουμένη τὰ βαρβαρικὰ καὶ προξενοῦσα φιλίας βασιλέων καὶ πραγμάτων ἐμπείρους ποιοῦσα πολλῶν.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">πολλοὶ γὰρ πλουτεῦσι κακοί, ἀγαθοὶ δὲ πένονται·</l> <l>ἀλλʼ ἡμεῖς αὐτοῖς οὐ διαμειψόμεθα</l> <l>τῆς ἀρετῆς τὸν πλοῦτον· ἐπεὶ τὸ μὲν ἔμπεδον αἰεί,</l> <l>χρήματα δʼ ἀνθρώπων ἄλλοτε ἄλλος ἔχει.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 15 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">πρῶτα μὲν εὐχώμεσθα Διῒ Κρονίδῃ βασιλῆϊ</l> <l>θεσμοῖς τοῖσδε τύχην ἀγαθὴν καὶ κῦδος ὀπάσσαι.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Fragm. 31 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">ἐκ νεφέλης πέλεται χιόνος μένος ἠδὲ χαλάζης·</l> <l>βροντὴ δʼ ἐκ λαμπρᾶς γίνεται ἀστεροπῆς.</l> <l>ἐξ ἀνέμων δὲ θάλασσα ταράσσεται· ἢν δέ τις αὐτὴν</l> <l>μὴ κινῇ, πάντων ἐστὶ δικαιοτάτη.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 9. 1-2, Frag. 12 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>καὶ ὅλως ἔοικεν ἡ Θάλεω μόνου σοφία τότε περαιτέρω τῆς χρείας ἐξικέσθαι τῇ θεωρίᾳ· τοῖς δὲ ἄλλοις ἀπὸ τῆς πολιτικῆς ἀρετῆς τοὔνομα τῆς σοφίας ὑπῆρξε.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">αὐτὸς κῆρυξ ἦλθον ἀφʼ ἱμερτῆς Σαλαμῖνος,</l> <l>κόσμον ἐπέων ᾠδὴν ἀντʼ ἀγορῆς θέμενος.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 1 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">Αἴας δʼ ἐκ Σαλαμῖνος ἄγεν δυοκαίδεκα νῆας,</l> <l>στῆσε δʼ ἄγων ἵνʼ Ἀθηναίων ἵσταντο φάλαγγες.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Hom. Il. 2.557-558</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="troch">εἰ δὲ γῆς (φησίν) ἐφεισάμην</l> <l>πατρίδος, τυραννίδος δὲ καὶ βίης ἀμειλίχου</l> <l>οὐ καθηψάμην μιάνας καὶ καταισχύνας κλέος,</l> <l>οὐδὲν αἰδεῦμαι· πλέον γὰρ ὧδε νικήσειν δοκέω πάντας ἀνθρώπους.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 32 (Bergk).</bibl> </cit>ὅθεν εὔδηλον ὅτι καὶ πρὸ τῆς νομοθεσίας μεγάλην δόξαν εἶχεν.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="troch">οὐκ ἔφυ Σόλων βαθύφρων οὐδὲ βουλήεις ἀνήρ·</l> <l>ἐσθλὰ γὰρ θεοῦ διδόντος αὐτὸς οὐκ ἐδέξατο.</l> <l>περιβαλὼν δʼ ἄγραν ἀγασθεὶς οὐκ ἐπέσπασεν μέγα</l> <l>δίκτυον, θυμοῦ θʼ ἁμαρτῇ καὶ φρενῶν ἀποσφαλείς.</l> <l>ἤθελον<note anchored="true" place="unspecified" resp="editor" xml:lang="eng"> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἤθελον, ἀσκὸς</foreign> Bergk, with the better MSS.: <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἤθελεν, αὐτός</foreign> (<gloss>he</gloss> (Solon) <gloss>would have been willing; himself</gloss>).</note> γάρ κεν κρατήσας, πλοῦτον ἄφθονον λαβὼν</l> <l>καὶ τυραννεύσας Ἀθηνῶν μοῦνον ἡμέραν μίαν,</l> <l>ἀσκὸς<note anchored="true" place="unspecified" resp="editor" xml:lang="eng"> <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἤθελον, ἀσκὸς</foreign> Bergk, with the better MSS.: <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἤθελεν, αὐτός</foreign> (<gloss>he</gloss> (Solon) <gloss>would have been willing; himself</gloss>).</note> ὕστερον δεδάρθαι κἀπιτετρῖφθαι γένος.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 33 (Bergk).</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="iamb">ὁμοῦ βίην τε καὶ δίκην συναρμόσας.</l> </quote> <note anchored="true" place="unspecified" resp="editor" xml:lang="eng">Fragment 36, verse 14 (Bergk); verse 16 of the longer fragment now found in Aristotle’s <title>Const. of Athens</title>, chapter xii. 4, where we have <foreign xml:lang="grc">κράτει νόμου, βίην τε κτλ</foreign>.</note> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 36. 14 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>ὅθεν ὕστερον ἐρωτηθεὶς εἰ τοὺς ἀρίστους Ἀθηναίοις νόμους ἔγραψεν,

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="iamb">ὅρους ἀνεῖλε πολλαχῆ πεπηγότας·</l> <l>πρόσθεν δὲ δουλεύουσα, νῦν ἐλευθέρα·</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 36. 4-5 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>καὶ τῶν ἀγωγίμων πρὸς ἀργύριον γεγονότων πολιτῶν τοὺς μὲν ἀνήγαγεν ἀπὸ ξένης,

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="iamb">γλῶσσαν οὐκέτʼ Ἀττικὴν</l> <l>ἱέντας, ὡς ἂν πολλαχῆ πλανωμένους·</l> <l>τοὺς δʼ ἐνθάδʼ αὐτοῦ δουλίην ἀεικέα ἔχοντας</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Frag. 36. 9-12 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>ἐλευθέρους φησὶ ποιῆσαι.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="troch">χαῦνα μὲν τότʼ ἐφράσαντο, νῦν δέ μοι χολούμενοι</l> <l>λοξὸν ὀφθαλμοῖς ὁρῶσι πάντες ὥστε δήϊον.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 34 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>καίτοι φησὶν ὡς, εἴ τις ἄλλος ἔσχε τὴν αὐτὴν δύναμιν,

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="iamb">οὐκ ἂν κατέσχε δῆμον, οὐδʼ ἐπαύσατο,</l> <l>πρὶν ἀνταράξας, πῖαρ ἐξεῖλεν γάλα.</l> </quote> <note anchored="true" place="unspecified" resp="editor" xml:lang="eng">So the verses are now more correctly found in Aristotle (<title>Const. of Athens</title>, xii. 5, Sandys).</note> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon; Aristot. Ath. Pol. 12.5</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">δήμῳ μὲν γὰρ ἔδωκα τόσον κράτος ὅσσον ἀπαρκεῖ,</l> <l>τιμῆς οὔτʼ ἀφελὼν οὔτʼ ἐπορεξάμενος·</l> <l>οἳ δʼ εἶχον δύναμιν καὶ χρήμασιν ἦσαν ἀγητοί,</l> <l>καὶ τοῖς ἐφρασάμην μηδὲν ἀεικὲς ἔχειν.</l> <l>ἔστην δʼ ἀμφιβαλὼν κρατερὸν σάκος ἀμφοτέροισι·</l> <l>νικᾶν δʼ οὐκ εἴασʼ οὐδετέρους ἀδίκως.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 5 (Bergk); Aristot. Ath. Pol. 12.1</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote" type="drama"> <l met="iamb">εὖ γοῦν ὡς γαμεῖν ἔχεις τάλας,</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">authorship uncertain, Philoctetes; Nauck, Trag. Graec. Frag. (2), p. 841</bibl> </cit>καὶ νέον ἐν δωματίῳ πλουσίας πρεσβύτιδος, ὥσπερ οἱ πέρδικες, ἀπὸ συνουσίας παχυνόμενον ἐξανευρὼν μετοικίσει πρὸς παρθένον νύμφην ἀνδρὸς δεομένην. ταῦτα μὲν οὖν περὶ τούτων.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote" type="drama"> <l met="iamb">πολλοῖσι πολλήν, δὶς τοσοῖσδε πλείονα,</l> </quote> <note anchored="true" place="unspecified" resp="editor" xml:lang="eng">Following Nauck (<title>Trag. Graec. Frag.</title> <hi rend="superscript">2</hi>, p. 680): <foreign xml:lang="grc">πολλοῖς, τοσοῖσδε</foreign>.</note> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Euripides, unknown; Nauck, Trag. Graec. Frag. (2), p. 680</bibl> </cit>κατʼ Εὐριπίδην, καὶ τὸ μέγιστον, εἱλωτικοῦ πλήθους, ὃ βέλτιον ἦν μὴ σχολάζειν, ἀλλὰ τριβόμενον ἀεὶ καὶ πονοῦν ταπεινοῦσθαι, περικεχυμένου τῇ Λακεδαίμονι, καλῶς εἶχεν ἀσχολιῶν ἐπιπόνων καὶ βαναύσων ἀπαλλάξαντα τοὺς πολίτας συνέχειν ἐν τοῖς ὅπλοις, μίαν τέχνην ταύτην ἐκμανθάνοντας καὶ ἀσκοῦντας·

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote" type="drama"> <l met="iamb">πρὸς τοῦ Σόλωνος καὶ Δράκοντος οἷσι νῦν</l> <l>φρύγουσιν ἤδη τὰς κάχρυς τοῖς κύρβεσιν.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Cratinus, unknown; Kock, Com. Att. Frag. i. p. 94.</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">τοῦ μὲν φθίνοντος μηνός, τοῦ δʼ ἱσταμένοιο,</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Hom. Od. 14.162; Hom. Od. 19.307</bibl> </cit>τὴν δʼ ἐφεξῆς ἡμέραν νουμηνίαν ἐκάλεσε. τὰς δʼ ἀπʼ εἰκάδος οὐ προστιθείς, ἀλλʼ ἀφαιρῶν καὶ ἀναλύων, ὥσπερ τὰ φῶτα τῆς σελήνης ἑώρα, μέχρι τριακάδος ἠρίθμησεν.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">Νείλου ἐπὶ προχοῇσι Κανωβίδος ἐγγύθεν ἀκτῆς.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 7 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>χρόνον δέ τινα καὶ τοῖς περὶ Ψένωφιν τὸν Ἡλιουπολίτην καὶ Σῶγχιν τὸν Σαΐτην, λογιωτάτοις οὖσι τῶν ἱερέων, συνεφιλοσόφησε· παρʼ ὧν καὶ τὸν Ἀτλαντικὸν ἀκούσας λόγον, ὡς Πλάτων φησίν, ἐπεχείρησε διὰ ποιήματος ἐξενεγκεῖν εἰς τοὺς Ἕλληνας.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">νῦν δὲ (φησί) σὺ μὲν Σολίοισι πολὺν χρόνον ἐνθάδʼ ἀνάσσων</l> <l>τήνδε πόλιν ναίοις καὶ γένος ὑμέτερον·</l> <l>αὐτὰρ ἐμὲ ξὺν νηῒ θοῇ κλεινῆς ἀπὸ νήσου</l> <l>ἀσκηθῆ πέμποι Κύπρις ἰοστέφανος·</l> <l>οἰκισμῷ δʼ ἐπὶ τῷδε χάριν καὶ κῦδος ὀπάζοι</l> <l>ἐσθλὸν καὶ νόστον πατρίδʼ ἐς ἡμετέρην.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 19 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">εἰς γὰρ γλῶσσαν ὁρᾶτε καὶ εἰς ἔπη αἱμύλοι ἀνδρός.</l> <l>ὑμῶν δʼ εἷς μὲν ἕκαστος ἀλώπεκος ἴχνεσι βαίνει,</l> <l>σύμπασιν δʼ ὑμῖν χαῦνος ἔνεστι νόος.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 11. 7, 5, 6 (Bergk). Plutarch has changed the order; Bekker and Cobet restore it.</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">εἰ δὲ πεπόνθατε λυγρὰ διʼ ὑμετέρην κακότητα,</l> <l>μή τι θεοῖς τούτων μῆνιν ἐπαμφέρετε.</l> <l>αὐτοὶ γὰρ τούτους ηὐξήσατε ῥύματα δόντες,</l> <l>καὶ διὰ ταῦτα κακὴν ἔσχετε δουλοσύνην.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 11. 7, 5, 6 (Bergk). Plutarch has changed the order; Bekker and Cobet restore it.</bibl> </cit>
<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">γηράσκω δʼ αἰεὶ πολλὰ διδασκόμενος·</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 18 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>καί,

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote rend="blockquote"> <l met="dact">ἔργα δὲ Κυπρογενοῦς νῦν μοι φίλα καὶ Διονύσου</l> <l>καὶ Μουσέων, ἃ τίθησʼ ἀνδράσιν εὐφροσύνας.</l> </quote> <bibl xml:lang="eng">Solon, Frag. 26 (Bergk)</bibl> </cit>

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Att. 13.42.2"> <title>ad Att.</title> xiii. 42, 2</bibl>), the Nones being the fifth of January. Strictly speaking, only the first day of the month was called the Calends, but Plutarch seems to call the opening days of the new official year
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Planc. 26"> <title>Or. pro Plancio</title>, 26</bibl>. This was in the succeeding year (74 B.C.).

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Div. Caec. 1"> <title>Divinatio in Caecilium</title> </bibl>) only the first two were delivered; the others were compiled after the verdict had been pronounced.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Plut. Crass. 13.3"> <title>Crassus</title>, xiii 3</bibl>. Cicero’s treatise on his consulship, there referred to, was written in Greek, and is not extant.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Sul. 18"> <title>pro Sulla</title> (6, 18)</bibl> and Sallust’s
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Sal. Cat. 28"> <title>Catiline</title> (28)</bibl> it appears that the names of these would-be murders were Caius Cornelius and Lucius Vargunteius.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Pis. 6"> <title>in Pisonem</title>, 3, 6</bibl>, he says that Quintus Catulus gave him the title in the Senate.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Fam. 16.21.6"> <title>ad fam.</title> xvi. 21, 6</bibl>), says that he had found Gorgias useful as a teacher of declamation, but had dismissed him in obedience to his father’s positive command.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Plut. Caes. 10.7"> <title>Caesar</title>, x. 7</bibl>. Each juror was provided with three tablets, on one of which was marked A (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Att. 2.18.3"> <title>ad Att.</title> ii. 18, 3</bibl>), it was Caesar who made the request.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Red. Pop. 1.1"> <title>post red. ad Quir.</title> 3, 8</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Plut. Cic. 30.1">xxx. 1</bibl> and below in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Red. Sen. 39">Cicero, <title>post red. in sen.</title> 15, 39.</bibl>
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Cic. Fam. 2.10.2">Cicero, <title>ad fam.</title> ii. 10, 2 f.</bibl>

The reply here given is; (a) if a group of footpads had in fact been engaged in the murder, the passers-by would have run away. (b) The passers-by would in that case have been unable to supply information about the identity of the criminals. (c) As no passer-by has come forward with such information, all the passers-by must have run away. (d) It follows from (a) that the murderers must have been a group of footpads. A portentous petitio principii, which of course entirely neglects the fact that passers-by had come forward with very different information.

Thus, the ancient Egyptians believed that, on his way to the spirit land, the soul of a dead person was met by a goddess (Hathor, Nouit, or Nit), who offered him fruits, bread, and water, and that, if he accepted them, he could return to earth no more. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. A. 7.761">Serv. Verg. A. 7.761</bibl>, the period of Apollo's service was not one but nine years. In making this statement Servius, or his authority, probably had before him a Greek author, who mentioned an
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Censorinus, De die natali 18.5</bibl>), and the period of banishment for a homicide was regularly a year. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Nicolaus Damascenus, Frag 20 (Fragmenta Historicorum Graccorum, ed. C. Müller, iii.369)</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">ἀπεναυτίσαι</foreign> </bibl>. Hence it seems probable that, though in later times the period of a homicide's banishment was a single ordinary year, it may formerly have been a “great year,” or period of eight ordinary years. It deserves to be noted that any god who had forsworn himself by the Styx had to expiate his fault by silence and fasting for a full year, after which he was banished the company of the gods for nine years (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hes. Th. 793">Hes. Th. 793-804ff.</bibl>); and further that any man who partook of human flesh in the rites of Lycaean Zeus was supposed to be turned into a wolf for nine years. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Augustine, De civitate Dei xviii.17</bibl>. In the present passage of Apollodorus, the addition of a month to the eight years' period creates a difficulty which I am unable to explain. Ancient mathematicians defined a “great year” as the period at the end of which the sun, moon, and planets again occupy the same positions relatively to each other which they occupied at the beginning; but on the length of the period opinions were much divided. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Astr. ii.3</bibl>, and the Scholiast on the Aratea of Germanicus.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 56</bibl> adds that the seer Phrasius, who advised the sacrifice, was a brother of Pygmalion. Herodotus, without mentioning Busiris, scouts the story on the ground that human sacrifices were utterly alien to the spirit of Egyptian religion (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hdt. 2.45">Hdt. 2.45</bibl>). Isocrates also discredited the tradition, in so far as it relates to Herakles, because Herakles was four generations younger, and Busiris more than two hundred years older, than Perseus. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Isoc. 11.15">Isoc. 11.15</bibl>. Yet there are grounds for thinking that the Greek tradition was substantially correct. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Plut. Isis et Osiris 30, 33</bibl>). But redhaired men would commonly be foreigners, in contrast to the black-haired natives of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Diod. 1.88.5</bibl>) in confirmation of the Greek tradition, and he tells us that the redhaired men were sacrificed at the grave of Osiris, though this statement may be an inference from his etymology of the name Busiris, which he explains to mean “grave of Osiris.” The etymology is correct, Busiris being a Greek rendering of the Egyptian Asir “place of Osiris.” See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. Wiedemann, <title>Herodots Zweites Buch</title> (Leipsic, 1890), p. 213</bibl>. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Porphyry, De abstinentia iii.35</bibl>. Sextus Empiricus even speaks of human sacrifices in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Sextus Empiricus, p. 173, ed. Bekker</bibl>. Seleucus wrote a special treatise on human sacrifices in

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Athenaeus iv.72, p. 172 D</bibl>). <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>The Magic Art and the Evolution of Kings</title>, i.344ff., 352ff.</bibl>); and in ancient

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ammianus Marcellinus xxviii.5.14</bibl>); hence it would not be surprising if in extreme cases they were put to death. Busiris was the theme of a Satyric play by Euripides. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Ap. Rhod., Argon. iv.1396</bibl> calls him Iphidamas, and adds “the herald Chalbes and the attendants” to the list of those slain by Herakles.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Aesch. Eum. 732">Aesch. Eum. 732(762)ff.</bibl> And Euripides makes Hector declare that the foreigners who had fought in defence of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild</title>, i.294ff.</bibl> The references in Greek legend to men who habitually relieved strangers of their heads, which they added to their collection of skulls, may point to the former existence among the Greeks of a practice of collecting human skulls for the purpose of securing the ghostly protection of their late owners. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Jebb on Soph. El. 445, with the Appendix, pp. 211ff.</bibl> The practice is perhaps illustrated by an original drawing in the Ambrosian manuscript of the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 10.314">Hom. Il. 10.314ff.</bibl>); in the drawing the corpse of the slain Dolon is depicted shorn of its feet and hands, which lie beside it, while Ulysses holds Dolon's severed head in his hand. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Annali dell' Instituto di Correspondenza Archeologica</title> (Rome, 1875), tav. d'agg. R.</bibl>;

It appears to be a widespread belief that the ghost of one who has died a violent death is dangerous to his slayer, but that he can be rendered powerless for mischief by maiming his body in such a way as would have disabled him in life. For example, some of the Australian aborigines used to cut off the thumbs of the right hands of dead enemies to prevent their ghosts from throwing spears. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. Oldfield, “The Aborigines of Australia,” <title>Transactions of the Ethnological Society of London</title>, iii. (1865) p. 287</bibl>. In Travancore the spirits of murderers who have been hanged are thought to be very mischievous; hence, in order to prevent them from doing harm, it used to be customary to cut off the heels of the criminal with a sword or to hamstring him as he swung on the gallows. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">S. Mateer, <title>The Land of Charity</title> (London, (1871), pp. 203ff.</bibl> In

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Manuk Abeghian, <title>Der armenische Volksglaube</title> (Leipsig, 1899), p. 11</bibl>. In some parts of West Africa it is similarly customary to disinter and decapitate a corpse of a person whose ghost is supposed to be causing sickness, “because the deceased, having his head cut off, will not have the same strength as before, and consequently will not be in a position to trouble him (the patient).” See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">J. B. Labat, <title>Relation Historique de l'Ethiopie Occidentale</title> (Paris, 1732), i.208</bibl>.

Now of all the things in the world the dearest to Dionysus were the ivy, the vine, and the myrtle; so of these he sent the myrtle, and that is why the initiated in his rites wreathed their brows with myrtle leaves. The Chins of Northeastern India think that “one of the worst omens that it is possible to see is two snakes copulating, and a man who sees this is not supposed to return to his house or to speak to anyone until the next sun has risen” (

Rangoon, 1896, p. 199</bibl>). “It is considered extremely unlucky for a Chin to come upon two snakes copulating, and to avoid ill-fortune he must remain outside the village that night, without eating cooked food; the next morning he may proceed to his house, but, on arrival there, must kill a fowl and, if within his means, hold a feast. If a man omits these precautions and is found out, he is liable to pay compensation of a big
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">W. R. Head, <title>Haka Chin Customs</title>, Rangoon, 1917, p. 44</bibl>). In the

Similarly in Southern India there prevails “a superstitious belief that, if a person sees two crows engaged in sexual congress, he will die unless one of his relations sheds tears. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">E. Thurston, op. cit. p. 278</bibl>). A similar belief as to the dire effect of seeing crows coupling, and a similar mode of averting the calamity, are reported in the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius, Theb. ix.455-539</bibl>, Hippomedon was overwhelmed by a cloud of Theban missiles after being nearly drowned in the river Ismenus.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. v.126</bibl>. All these writers say that it was Amphiaraus, not Tydeus, who killed as well as decapitated Melanippus. Pausanias also (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.18.1">Paus. 9.18.1</bibl>) represents Melanippus as slain by Amphiaraus. Hence Heyne was perhaps right in rejecting as an interpolation the words “who, wounded though he was, had killed him.” See the Critical Note. The story is told also by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius, Theb. viii.717-767</bibl> in his usual diffuse style; but according to him it was Capaneus, not Amphiaraus, who slew and beheaded Melanippus and brought the gory head to Tydeus. The story of Tydeus's savagery is alluded to more than once by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ovid, Ibis 427ff., 515ff.</bibl>, that curious work in which the poet has distilled the whole range of ancient mythology for the purpose of commination. With this tradition of cannibalism on the field of battle we may compare the custom of the ancient Scythians, who regularly decapitated their enemies in battle and drank of the blood of the first man they slew (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hdt. 4.64">Hdt. 4.64</bibl>). It has indeed been a common practice with savages to swallow some part of a slain foe in order with the blood, or flesh, or brains to acquire the dead man's valour. See for example
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">L. A. Millet-Mureau, <title>Voyage de la Perouse autour du Monde</title> (Paris, 1797), ii.272</bibl> (as to the Californian Indians);

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Fay-Cooper Cole, <title>The Wild Tribes of Davao District, Mindanao</title> (Chicago, 1913), pp. 94, 189</bibl> (as to the Philippine Islanders). I have cited many more instances in

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild</title>, ii.148ff.</bibl> The story of the brutality of Tydeus to Melanippus may contain a reminiscence of a similar custom. From the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. v.126</bibl> we learn that the story was told by Pherecydes, whom Apollodorus may be following in the present passage. The grave of Melanippus was on the road from
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.18.1">Paus. 9.18.1</bibl>), but Clisthenes, tyrant of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hdt. 5.67">Hdt. 5.67</bibl>. It is probable that Clisthenes, in “fetching Melanippus,” transferred the hero's bones to the new shrine at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hdt. 1.67">Hdt. 1.67ff.</bibl>). Pausanias mentions many instances of the practice. See the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Index to my translation of Pausanias, s.v. “Bones,” vol. vi. p. 31</bibl>. It was, no doubt, unusual to bury bones in the Prytaneum, where was the Common Hearth of the city (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Frazer, note on Paus. viii.53.9, vol. iv. pp. 441ff.</bibl>); but at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.9.5">Paus. 8.9.5</bibl>); and the graves of not a few heroes and heroines were shown in Greek temples. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Clement of Alexandria, Protrept. iii.45, pp. 39ff., ed. Potter</bibl>. The subject of relic worship in antiquity is exhaustively treated by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius, Theb. vii.789-823</bibl>. The reference to Periclymenus clearly proves that Apollodorus had here in mind the first of these passages of Pindar. Pausanias repeatedly mentions Baton as the charioteer of Amphiaraus (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 10.10.3">Paus. 10.10.3</bibl>). Amphiaraus was believed to be swallowed up alive, with his chariot and horses, and so to descend to the nether world. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 49 (First Vatican Mythographer 152)</bibl>. Hence Sophocles speaks of him as reigning fully alive in Hades (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Soph. El. 836">Soph. Elec. 836ff.</bibl>). Moreover, Amphiaraus was deified (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Cicero, De divinatione i.40.88</bibl>), and as a god he had a famous oracle charmingly situated in a little glen near Oropus in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Frazer, commentary on Paus., vol. ii. pp. 466ff.</bibl>). The exact spot where Amphiaraus disappeared into the earth was shown not far from
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.8.3">Paus. 9.8.3</bibl>. As the ground was split open by a thunderbolt to receive Amphiaraus (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. N. 10">Pind. N. 10.8(13)ff.</bibl>), the enclosure with pillars in it was doubtless one of those little sanctuaries, marked off by a fence, which the Greeks always instituted on ground struck by lightning. See Frazer on Apollod. 3.7.1.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 22.346">Hom. Il. 22.346ff.</bibl>), without giving particulars to the quaint and curious myth with which he was probably acquainted. That myth, one of the most savage of all the stories of ancient
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. 23.346</bibl>. The story was told at two places in the highlands of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Frazer, commentary on Pausanias, vol. iv. pp. 406ff.</bibl> According to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.43.1">Paus. 1.43.1</bibl>) that he died at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 242</bibl> tells a strange story that Adrastus and his son Hipponous threw themselves into the fire in obedience to an oracle of Apollo.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Aesch. Seven 1005">Aesch. Seven 1005ff.</bibl> A different version of the story is told by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 72</bibl>. According to him, when Antigone was caught in the act of performing funeral rites for her brother Polynices, Creon handed her over for execution to his son Haemon, to whom she had been betrothed. But Haemon, while he pretended to put her to death, smuggled her out of the way, married her, and had a son by her. In time the son grew up and came to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Supp. 1">Eur. Supp. 1ff.</bibl>). In favour of the latter version it may be said that the graves of the fallen leaders were shown at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Plut. Thes. 29">Plut. Thes. 29</bibl>); while the graves of the common soldiers were at Eleutherae, which is on the borders of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Plut. Thes. 29">Plut. Thes. 29</bibl>). Tradition varied also on the question how the Athenians obtained the permission of the Thebans to bury the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.39.2">Paus. 1.39.2</bibl>) and by the patriotic Boeotian Plutarch, who expressly rejects Euripides's account of the Theban defeat. Isocrates, with almost incredible fatuity, adopts both versions in different passages of his writings and defends himself for so doing (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Isoc. 12.168">Isoc. 12.168-174</bibl>). Lysias, without expressly mentioning the flight of Adrastus to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.17.1">Paus. 1.17.1</bibl>, with my note (vol. ii. pp. 143ff.);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius, Theb. xii.481-505</bibl>. It is mentioned in a late Greek inscription found at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">G. Kaibel, Epigrammata Graeca ex lapidibus conlecta 792</bibl>). The altar, though not mentioned by early writers, was in later times one of the most famous spots in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Philostratus, Epist. 39</bibl>). In this fancy he perhaps copied
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius, Theb. xii.800ff.</bibl>, with the note of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Martial iv.75.5</bibl>. Capaneus had been killed by a thunderbolt as he was mounting a ladder at the siege of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.6.7">Apollod. 3.6.7</bibl>. Hence his body was deemed sacred and should have been buried, not burned, and the grave fenced off; whereas the other bodies were all consumed on a single pyre. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Ba. 6">Eur. Ba. 6-11</bibl>. Yet, inconsistently with the foregoing passage, Euripides appears afterwards to assume that the body of Capaneus was burnt on a pyre (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Supp. 1000">Eur. Supp. 1000ff.</bibl>). The rule that a person killed by a thunderbolt should be buried, not burnt, is stated by
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Pliny, Nat. Hist. ii.145</bibl> and alluded to by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tertullian, Apologeticus 48</bibl>. An ancient Roman law, attributed to Numa, forbade the celebration of the usual obsequies for a man who had been killed by lightning. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Festus, s.v. “Occisum,” p. 178, ed. C. O. Müller</bibl>. It is true that these passages refer to the Roman usage, but the words of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Supp. 934">Eur. Supp. 934-938</bibl> seem to imply that the Greek practice was similar, and this is confirmed by Artemidorus, who says that the bodies of persons killed by lightning were not removed but buried on the spot (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Artemidorus, Onirocrit. ii.9</bibl>). The same writer tells us that a man struck by lightning was not deemed to be disgraced, nay, he was honoured as a god; even slaves killed by lightning were approached with respect, as honoured by Zeus, and their dead bodies were wrapt in fine garments. Such customs are to some extent explained by the belief that Zeus himself descended in the flash of lightning; hence whatever the lightning struck was naturally regarded as holy. Places struck by lightning were sacred to Zeus the Descender (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Frazer, Paus. vol. iii. p. 565, vol. v. p. 614</bibl>). Compare

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">H. Useher, “Keraunos,” <title>Kleine Schriften</title>, iv.477ff.</bibl>, (who quotes from Clemens Romanus and Cyrillus more evidence of the worship of persons killed by lightning);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Chr. Blinkenberg, <title>The Thunder-weapon in Religion and Folklore</title> (Cambridge, 1911), pp. 110ff.</bibl> Among the Ossetes of the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Julius von Klaproth, <title>Reise in den Kaukasus und nach Georgien</title> (Halle and Berlin, 1814), ii.606</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. von Haxthausen, <title>Transkaukasia</title> (Leipsig, 1856), ii.21ff.</bibl> Similarly the Kafirs of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">“Mr. Warner's Notes,” in Col. Maclean's <title>Compendium of Kafir Laws and Customs</title> (Cape Town, 1866), pp. 82-84</bibl>. Sometimes, however, the ghosts of persons who have been killed by lightning are deemed to be dangerous. Hence the Omahas used to slit the soles of the feet of such corpses to prevent their ghosts from walking about. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">J. Owen Dorsey, “A Study of Siouan Cults,” <title>Eleventh Annual Report of the Bureau of Ethnology</title> (Washington, 1894), p. 420</bibl>. For more evidence of special treatment accorded to the bodies of persons struck dead by lightning, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. B. Ellis, <title>The Ewe-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast</title> (London, 1890), p. 39ff.</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. B. Ellis, <title>The Yoruba-speaking Peoples of the Slave Coast</title> (London, 1894), p. 49</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Rev. J. H. Weeks, “Notes on some customs of the Lower Congo people,” <title>Folk-Lore</title>, xx. (1909), p. 475</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. L. Kitching, <title>On the backwaters of the Nile</title> (London, 1912), pp. 264ff.</bibl> Among the Barundi of Central Africa, a man or woman who has been struck, but not killed, by lightning becomes thereby a priest or priestess of the god Kiranga, whose name he or she henceforth bears and of whom he or she is deemed a bodily representative. And any place that has been struck by lightning is enclosed, and the trunk of a banana-tree or a young fig-tree is set up in it to serve as the temporary abode of the deity who manifested himself in the lightning. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 70</bibl>. There was an epic poem on the subject, called
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Biographi Graeci, ed. A. Westermann, pp. 42ff.</bibl>), but others attributed it to Antimachus (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Epicorum Graecorum Fragmenta, ed. G. Kinkel, pp. 13ff.</bibl> Aeschylus and Sophocles both wrote tragedies on the same subject and with the same title,

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.8.6">Paus. 9.8.6</bibl>. As to Cadmus and Harmonia in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.33.1">Paus. 9.33.1</bibl>, who says that the grave of Tiresias was at the spring. But there was also a cenotaph of the seer on the road from

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 73</bibl>. Sophocles and Euripides both wrote tragedies called
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>The Fragments of Sophocles</title>, ed. A. C. Pearson, vol. i. pp. 68ff.</bibl>
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Prop. 1.15">Prop. i.15.19</bibl> call her Alphesiboea.

The notion that the shedding of blood, especially the blood of a kinsman, is an offence to the earth, which consequently refuses to bear crops, seems to have been held by the ancient Hebrews, as it is still apparently held by some African peoples. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.24.8">Paus. 8.24.8ff.</bibl> As to the formation of new land by the deposit of alluvial soil at the mouth of the Achelous, compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Athenaeus vi.22, p. 232 DF</bibl>, where the words of the oracle are quoted.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.24.7">Paus. 8.24.7</bibl>. A quiet resting-place for the matricide among the solemn Arcadian mountains after the long fever of the brain and the long weary wanderings. The valley, which I have visited, somewhat resembles a
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.24.10">Paus. 8.24.10</bibl> calls them Temenus and Axion.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.41.2">Paus. 9.41.2</bibl>, it was the sons of Phegeus, not the sons of Alcmaeon, who dedicated the necklace at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Parthenius, Narrat. 25</bibl> (who quotes Phylarchus as his authority);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Athenaeus vi.22, p. 232 DE</bibl> (who quotes the thirtieth book of the history of Ephorus as his authority).
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.24.9">Paus. 8.24.9</bibl>, who similarly derive the name of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Thuc. 2.68.3">Thuc. 2.68.3</bibl>, who represents the founder Amphilochus as the son of Amphiaraus, and therefore as the brother, not the son, of Alcmaeon. As to Amphilochus, son of Amphiaraus, see above,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes (Scholiast on Lycophron 481)</bibl>, who mentions Apollodorus by name as his authority. For another and different list of Lycaon's sons, see

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.3.1">Paus. 8.3.1ff.</bibl>, who calls Nyctimus the eldest son of Lycaon, whereas Apollodorus calls him the youngest (see below). That the wife of Pelasgus and mother of Lycaon was Cyllene is affirmed by the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Nicolaus Damascenus, Frag. 43 (Fragmenta Historicorum Graecorum, ed. C. Müller, iii.378</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Λυκάων</foreign> </bibl>): “Lycaon, son of Pelasgus and king of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 176</bibl>, who adds that Zeus in his wrath upset the table, killed the sons of Lycaon with a thunderbolt, and turned Lycaon himself into a wolf. According to this version of the legend, which Apollodorus apparently accepted, Lycaon was a righteous king, who ruled wisely like his father Pelasgus before him (see

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.1.4">Paus. 8.1.4-6</bibl>), but his virtuous efforts to benefit his subjects were frustrated by the wickedness and impiety of his sons, who by exciting the divine anger drew down destruction on themselves and on their virtuous parent, and even imperilled the existence of mankind in the great flood. But according to another, and perhaps more generally received, tradition, it was King Lycaon himself who tempted his divine guest by killing and dishing up to him at table a human being; and, according to some, the victim was no other than the king's own son Nyctimus. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Clement of <name type="place" key="perseus,Alexandria">Alexandria</name>, Protrept. ii.36, p. 31, ed. Potter</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Arnobius, Adversus Nationes iv.24</bibl>. Some, however, said that the victim was not the king's son, but his grandson Arcas, the son of his daughter Callisto by Zeus. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholia in Caesaris Germanici Aratea, p. 387 (in Martianus Capella, ed. Fr. Eyssenhardt)</bibl>. According to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 1.218">Ov. Met. 1.218ff.</bibl>, the victim was a Molossian hostage. Others said simply that Lycaon set human flesh before the deity. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i.5 (First Vatican Mythographer 17)</bibl>. For this crime Zeus changed the wicked king into a wolf, according to Hyginus, Ovid, the Scholiast on Caesar Germanicus, and the First Vatican Mythographer; but, on the other hand, Clement of Alexandria, Nonnus, Eratosthenes, and Arnobius say nothing of such a transformation. The upsetting of the table by the indignant deity is recorded by
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Ast. ii.4</bibl> and Apollodorus. A somewhat different account of the tragical occurrence is given by Pausanias, who says (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.2.3">Paus. 8.2.3</bibl>) that Lycaon brought a human babe to the altar of Lycaean Zeus, after which he was immediately turned into a wolf. These traditions were told to explain the savage and cruel rites which appear to have been performed in honour of Lycaean Zeus on Mount Lycaeus down to the second century of our era or later. It seems that a human victim was sacrificed, and that his inward parts (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.2.6">Paus. 8.2.6</bibl>. According to another account, reported by Varro on the authority of a Greek writer Euanthes, the werewolf was chosen by lot, hung his clothes on an oak tree, swam across a pool, and was then transformed into a wolf and herded with wolves for nine years, afterwards recovering his human shape if in the interval he had not tasted the flesh of man. In this account there is no mention of cannibalism. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Augustine, De civitate Dei xviii.17</bibl>. A certain Arcadian boxer, named Damarchus, son of Dinnytas, who won a victory at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 6.8.2">Paus. 6.8.2</bibl>. However, the transformation was recorded by a Greek writer, Scopas, in his history of Olympic victors, who called the boxer Demaenatus, and said that his change of shape was caused by his partaking of the inward parts of a boy slain in the Arcadian sacrifice to Lycaean Zeus. Scopas also spoke of the restoration of the boxer to the human form in the tenth year, and mentioned that his victory in boxing at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Augustine, De civitate Dei xviii.17</bibl>. The continuance of human sacrifice in the rites of Lycaean Zeus on Mount Lycaeus is hinted at by
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.38.7">Paus. 8.38.7</bibl> in the second century of our era, and asserted by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Porphyry, (De abstinentia ii.27: Eusebius, Praeparatio Evangelii, iv.16.6)</bibl> in the third century. From these fragmentary notices it is hardly possible to piece together a connected account of the rite; but the mention of the transformation of the cannibal into a wolf for eight or nine years suggests that the awful sacrifice was offered at intervals either of eight or of nine years. If the interval was eight years, it would point to the use of that eight years' cycle which played so important a part in the ancient calendar of the Greeks, and by which there is reason to think that the tenure of the kingship was in some places regulated. Perhaps the man who was supposed to be turned into a wolf acted as the priest, or even as the incarnation, of the Wolf God for eight or nine years till he was relieved of his office at the next celebration of the rites. The subject has been learnedly discussed by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. B. Cook (<title>Zeus</title>, i.63-99);</bibl>. He regards Lycaean Zeus as a god of light rather than of wolves, and for this view there is much to be said. See Frazer on Paus. 8.38.7 (vol. iv. pp. 385ff.). The view would be confirmed if we were sure that the solemn sacrifice was octennial, for the octennial period was introduced in order to reconcile solar and lunar time, and hence the religious rites connected with it would naturally have reference to the great celestial luminaries. As to the octennial period, see the note on

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 2.5.11">Apollod. 2.5.11</bibl>. But with this view of the festival it is difficult to reconcile the part played by wolves in the myth and ritual. We can hardly suppose with some late Greek writers, that the ancient Greek word for a year,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.31.5">Paus. 8.31.5</bibl>. The name is derived by Apollodorus from the Greek
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Libanius, in Westermann's Mythographi Graeci, Appendix Narrationum, 34, p. 374</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholia in Caesaris Germanici Aratea, p. 381, ed. F. Eyssenhardt</bibl> (in his edition of Martianus Capella);

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 5 (First Vatican Mythographer 17; vol. ii. p. 94, Second Vatican Mythographer 58)</bibl>. The transformation of Callisto into a bear is variously ascribed to the amorous Zeus himself, to the jealous Hera, and to the indignant Artemis. The descent of the Arcadians from a bear-woman through a son Arcas, whose name was popularly derived from the Greek
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Eur. Or. 1646</bibl>, Callisto, mother of Arcas, was a daughter of Ceteus by Stilbe.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.4.1">Paus. 8.4.1ff.</bibl> According to Pausanias, Arcas had three sons, Azas, Aphidas, and Elatus by Erato, a Dryad nymph; to Azas his father Arcas assigned the district of Azania, to Aphidas the city of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.4.10">Paus. 8.4.10</bibl>, who mentions only the first two of these four sons.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 14, 91 (First Vatican Mythographer 39; Second Vatican Mythographer 47)</bibl>. As Apollodorus points out, there was a difference of opinion as to the name of Atalanta's father. According to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis 215</bibl> and the First and Second Vatican Mythographers (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 54, 124</bibl>), he was Iasius; according to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ael., Var. Hist. xiii.1</bibl>, he was Iasion.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Prop. 1.1">Prop. i.1.10</bibl> seems to agree with Apollodorus that her father was Iasus, for he calls Atalanta by the patronymic Iasis. But according to

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 8.35.10">Paus. 8.35.10</bibl>, Hyginus, and Ovid, her father was Schoeneus. Hesiod also called him Schoeneus (see Apollodorus, below), and the later writers just mentioned probably accepted the name on his authority. According to Euripides, as we learn from Apollodorus (see below), the name of the heroine's father was Maenalus. The suckling of Atalanta by the bear, and the unsuccessful assault on her by the two centaurs, Hylaeus and Rhoecus, are described, with a wealth of picturesque detail, by Aelian (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ael., Var. Hist. xiii.1</bibl>), who does not, however, mention her wedding race. The suitor who won the coy maiden's hand by throwing down the golden apples is called Hippomenes by most writers (Theocritus, Hyginus, Ovid, Servius, First and Second Vatican Mythographers). Herein later writers may have followed Euripides, who, as we learn from Apollodorus (see below), also called the successful suitor Hippomanes. But by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Ars 2">Ovid, Ars Am. ii.188</bibl> the lover is called Milanion, which nearly agrees with the form Melanion adopted by Apollodorus. Pausanias seems also to have agreed with Apollodorus on this point, for he tells us (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.12.9">Apollod. 3.12.9</bibl>) that Parthenopaeus, who was a son of Atalanta (see below), had Melanion for his father.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 10.644">Ov. Met. 10.644ff.</bibl> the goddess brought the golden apples from her sacred field of Tamasus, the richest land in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 14 (First Vatican Mythographer 39)</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. A. 3.113">Serv. Verg. A. 3.113</bibl>; and the First Vatican Mythographer (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 14, (Fab. 39)</bibl>. The reason why the lovers were turned into a lion and a lioness for their impiety is explained by the ancient mythographers to be that lions do not mate with each other, but with leopards, so that after their transformation the lovers could never repeat the sin of which they had been guilty. For this curious piece of natural history they refer to Pliny's
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Pliny, Nat. Hist. viii.43</bibl>). What would have happened if the lion had similarly misbehaved with a leopardess is not mentioned by the natural historian.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.6.3">Apollod. 3.6.3</bibl>. According to others, the father of Parthenopaeus was neither Melanion nor Ares, but Meleager. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 54, 125 (First Vatican Mythographer 174; Second Vatican Mythographer 144)</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. G. 1.138">Serv. Verg. G. 1.138</bibl>, and
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholia in Caesaris Germanici Aratea, p. 397, ed. F. Eyssenhardt (in his edition of Martianus Capella)</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 73 (First Vatican Mythographer 234)</bibl>. There was a general agreement among the ancients as to the names of the seven Pleiades. Aratus, for example, gives the same names as Apollodorus and in the same order. However, with the exception of Maia, a different list of names is given by the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Theocritus xiii.25</bibl>, who tells us further, on the authority of Callimachus, that they were the daughters of the queen of the Amazons. As their father was commonly said to be Atlas, they were sometimes called Atlantides (Apollodorus, below;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hes. WD 382">Hes. WD 382</bibl>). But there was much diversity of opinion as to the origin of the name Pleiades. Some derived it from the name of their mother Pleione; but the most probable view appears to be that the name comes from

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. G. 1.138">Serv. Verg. G. 1.138</bibl>). With regard to the number of the Pleiades, it was generally agreed that there were seven of them, but that one was invisible, or nearly so, to the human eye. Of this invisibility two explanations were given. Some thought that Electra, as the mother of Dardanus, was so grieved at the fall of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. von Humboldt, <title>Cosmos</title>, translated by E. Sabine, iii.47ff.</bibl>

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 5.10.6">Paus. 5.10.6</bibl>. According to another account, Sterope or Asterope, as she is also called, was not the wife but the mother of Oenomaus by the god Ares. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 73 (First Vatican Mythographer 234)</bibl>.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>The Homeric Hymns</title>, ed. T. W. Allen and E. E. Sikes, pp. 130ff.</bibl> Among the other literary sources to which Apollodorus may have had recourse was perhaps Sophocles's satyric play

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Sophocles, Ichneutae 269 (<title>The Fragments of Sophocles</title>, ed. A. C. Pearson, ii.258)</bibl>. So Dionysus at birth is said to have been laid on a winnowing-fan (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. G. 1.166">Serv. Verg. G. 1.166</bibl>): hence he got the surname of “He of the Winnowing-fan” (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Plut. Isis et Osiris 35</bibl>). These traditions as to the gods merely reflected an ancient Greek custom of placing newborn children in winnowing-fans “as an omen of wealth and fruitfulness” (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Callimachus, Hymn 1.48 (Callimachea, ed. O. Schneider, i.109)</bibl>. As to the symbolism of the custom, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">W. Mannhardt, “Kind und Korn,” <title>Mythologische Forschungen</title>, pp. 351-374</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Miss J. E. Harrison, “Mystica Vannus Iacchi,” JHS xxiii. (1903), pp. 292-324</bibl>. The custom was not confined to ancient
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild</title>, i.5-11</bibl>. To quote a single example, among the Brahuis of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Denys Bray, <title>The Life-History of a Brāhūī</title>London, 1913, p. 13</bibl>). The substitution of a corn-sieve for a winnowing-fan seems to be common elsewhere.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 2.680">Ov. Met. 2.680ff.</bibl> The theft of cattle by the infant Hermes was the subject of Sophocles's satyric drama

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>The Fragments of Sophocles</title>, ed. A. C. Pearson, vol. i. pp. 224-270</bibl>. From this seemingly simple piece of mild buffoonery Miss J. E. Harrison would extract a ritual of serious and indeed solemn significance, of which, however, she admits that the author of the play was himself probably quite unconscious. See her learned essay in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Essays and Studies presented to William Ridgeway</title>, ed. E. C. Quiggin (Cambridge, 1913), pp. 136ff.</bibl>

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="HH 4.115">HH Herm. 115ff.</bibl> we are told that Hermes roasted the flesh of two oxen and divided it into twelve portions (for the twelve gods), but that in spite of hunger he ate none of it himself.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Sophocles, Ichneutae 278ff. (<title>The Fragments of Sophocles</title>, ed. A. C. Pearson, ii.259)</bibl>. In the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="HH 4.22">HH Herm. 22ff.</bibl>, the invention of the lyre by Hermes precedes his theft of the cattle.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="HH 4.185">HH Herm. 185ff.</bibl> it is to Onchestus in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="HH 4.213">HH Herm. 213ff.</bibl>, where it is said that Apollo discovered Hermes to be the thief through observing a certain long-winged bird.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="HH 4.511">HH Herm. 511ff.</bibl>, where, however, nothing is said about an attempt of Apollo to get the pipes from Hermes, or about an exchange of the pipes for the golden wand. However, there is a lacuna in the hymn after verse 526, and the missing passage may have contained the exchange in question and the request of Hermes for the gift of divination, both of which are mentioned by Apollodorus but omitted in the hymn as it stands at present. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Allen and Sikes on the HH Herm. 526ff., in their edition of the Homeric Hymns, p. 190</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="HH 4.552">HH Herm. 552ff.</bibl> The reference is to the divining pebbles called
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Callimachus, Hymn to Apollo 45, with the Scholiast</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Anecdota Graeca, ed. Bekker, i.265.11, s.v<foreign xml:lang="grc">Θριάσιον πεδίον.</foreign> </bibl>. According to one account, the divining pebbles were an invention of Athena, which so disgusted Apollo that Zeus caused that mode of divination to fall into discredit, though it had been in high repute before; and Apollo vented his spite at the practitioners of a rival art by saying that “There be many that cast pebbles, but few prophets.” See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Stephanus Byzantius, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Θρία</foreign> </bibl>. This tradition may perhaps be accepted as evidence that in time the simple mode of divination by pebbles went out of fashion, being cast into the shade by the far more stately and imposing ritual of the frenzied prophetesses at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Nonnus, in Westermann's Mythographi Graeci, Appendix Narrationum 67, p. 384</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Πυθώ</foreign> </bibl>. As to Greek divination by pebbles, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. Bouche-Leclercq, <title>Histoire de la Divination dans l'Antiquité</title>, i.192,ff.</bibl>; and
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.1.1">Paus. 3.1.1</bibl>, Eurotas was a son of Myles, who was a son of Lelex.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Nicander, Ther. 901ff., with the Scholiast on Lycophron 902</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 37, 135ff. (First Vatican Mythographer 117; Second Vatican Mythographer 181)</bibl>. The tomb of Hyacinth was shown at Amyclae under the great image of Apollo; a bronze door opened into the tomb, and sacrifices were there offered to him as a hero. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 1.9.5">Apollod. 1.9.5</bibl>, where Apollodorus represents Perieres as the son of Aeolus (compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 1.7.3">Apollod. 1.7.3</bibl>), though he adds that many people regarded him as the son of Cynortas. See below
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 4.2.7">Paus. 4.2.7</bibl> (who seems to have misunderstood the foregoing passage of Pindar);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Pind. P. 3.8(14)</bibl>, who quotes authorities on both sides: amongst the champions of Arsinoe were Asclepiades and an

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 4.31.12">Paus. 4.31.12</bibl>. Apollodorus apparently accepted the Messenian view. But on the other side a long array of authorities declared in favour of Coronis, and her claim to be the mother of the god had the powerful support of the priesthood of Aesculapius at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 17, 37 (First Vatican Mythographer 46, 115)</bibl>. Pausanias, who expressly rejects the claim of Arsinoe, quotes in favour of Coronis a Delphic oracle, which he regards as decisive: for who should know the true mother of Aesculapius better than his own father Apollo? The testimony of the deity for once was quite unambiguous. It ran thus:— “O born to be the world's great joy, Aesculapius, Offspring of love, whom Phlegyas' daughter, fair Coronis, bore to me in rugged
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 2.26.7">Paus. 2.26.7</bibl>. In modern times the stones of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">H. Collitz and F. Bechtel, <title>Sammlung der griechischen Dialekt-Inschriften</title>, iii.1, pp. 162ff., No. 3342</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. P. 3">Pind. P. 3.8(14)ff.</bibl> Compare the Scholiast on this passage of Pindar, especially

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Frazer, note on Paus. ii.17.11 (vol. iii. pp. 72ff.)</bibl>. Compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">D'Arcy Wentworth Thompson, <title>Glossary of Greek Birds</title>, p. 93</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Zenobius, Cent. i.18</bibl>, who probably copied Apollodorus. According to

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Ion 999">Eur. Ion 999ff.</bibl>, Pallas gave Erichthonius two drops of the Gorgon's blood, one of them a deadly poison, the other a powerful medicine for the healing of diseases.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 1.9.13">Apollod. 1.9.13</bibl>) may have been restored to life by Aesculapius. This conjecture is confirmed by a passage of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Sextus Empiricus (p. 658 ed. Bekker)</bibl>, where we read: “Stesichorus in his
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. P. 3">Pind. P. 3.54(96)ff., with the Scholiast</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Sextus Empiricus, p. 658, ed. Bekker</bibl> (who quotes as his authority Staphylus in his book on the Arcadians);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Eur. Alc. 1</bibl> (who quotes Apollodorus as his authority);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Lactantius Placidus on Statius, Theb. iv.434, vi.353(375)</bibl>. After his resurrection Hippolytus is said to have gone to dwell at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Verg. A. 7.761">Verg. A. 7.761ff.</bibl>, with the commentary of Servius;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Persius, Sat. vi.56, pp. 347ff., ed. O. Jahn</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 118 (Second Vatican Mythographer 128)</bibl>. The silence of Apollodorus as to this well-known Italian legend, which was told to account for the famous priesthood of Diana at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Eur. Alc. 1</bibl> (both these writers cite Panyasis as their authority);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Zenobius, Cent. i.18</bibl>, but as usual without acknowledgment. Compare Pherecydes, quoted by the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 17 (First Vatican Mythographer 46)</bibl>. According to

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Diod. 4.71.1-3</bibl> Aesculapius as a physician was so successful in his practice that the death-rate was perceptibly lowered, and Hades accused the doctor to Zeus of poaching on his preserves. The accusation angered Zeus, and he killed Aesculapius with a thunderbolt. According to Pherecydes, with whom Apollodorus agrees, the period of Apollo's servitude with Admetus was one year; according to Servius and the First Vatican Mythographer it was nine years. This suggests that the period may have been what was called a “great” or “eternal” year, which included eight ordinary years. See above,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.4.2">Apollod. 3.4.2</bibl>, with the note on
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 2.5.11">Apollod. 2.5.11</bibl>. According to one account the motive for Apollo's servitude was his love for Admetus. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Eur. Alc. 1</bibl>, quoting Rhianus as his authority. Apollo is said to have served Branchus as well as Admetus (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Philostratus, Epist. 57</bibl>), and we have seen that he served Laomedon. See above,

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Eur. Alc. 1</bibl>, it was not the Cyclopes but their sons whom Apollo slew. The passage of Pherecydes, as quoted by the Scholiast, runs as follows: “To him” (that is, to Admetus) “came Apollo, to serve him as a thrall for a year, at the command of Zeus, because Apollo had slain the sons of Brontes, of Steropes, and of Arges. He slew them out of spite at Zeus, because Zeus slew his son Aesculapius with a thunderbolt at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 284, 511</bibl>. Pausanias consistently represents Perieres as the son of Aeolus, and this tradition had the support of Hesiod (quoted by
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 284</bibl>). On the other hand Tzetzes represents Perieres as the son of Cynortes (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Lycophron 511</bibl>). Apollodorus here and elsewhere (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 1.9.5">Apollod. 1.9.5</bibl>) mentions both traditions without deciding between them. In two passages (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 1.9.5">Apollod. 1.9.5</bibl>) he asserts or implies that the father of Perieres was Aeolus; in another passage (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.10.3">Apollod. 3.10.3</bibl>) he asserts that the father of Perieres was Cynortes. In the present passage he seems to say that according to one tradition there were two men of the name of Perieres: one of them was the son of Aeolus and father of Aphareus and Leucippus; the other was the son of Cynortes and father of Oebalus, who married the nymph Batia and became by her the father of Tyndareus, Hippocoon, and Icarius. Pausanias says that Gorgophone, daughter of Perseus, first married Perieres and had by him two sons, Aphareus and Leucippus, and that after his death she married Oebalus, son of Cynortas (Cynortes), and had by him a son Tyndareus. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 4.2.4">Paus. 4.2.4</bibl>. Apollodorus, on the other hand, represents Perieres as the father not only of Aphareus and Leucippus, but also of Tyndareus and Icarius by Gorgophone, daughter of Perseus. See above,

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Lycophron 511</bibl>) agrees with him as to the sons, but makes Perieres the son of Cynortas instead the son of Aeolus. Thus there were two traditions as to the father of Tyndareus; according to one, his father was Perieres, according to the other, he was Oebalus. But the two traditions were agreed as to the mother of Tyndareus, whom they represented as Gorgophone, daughter of Perseus. According to another account, which may have been intended to reconcile the discrepant traditions as to the father of Tyndareus, Oebalus was the son of Perieres and the father of Tyndareus, Icarius, Arene, and the bastard Hippocoon, whom he had by Nicostrate. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. ii.581</bibl>. This account is mentioned, but apparently not accepted, by Apollodorus in the present passage, though he says nothing about the daughter Arene and the bastardy of Hippocoon. If we accept this last version of the genealogy, Tyndareus was descended both from Oebalus and Perieres, being the son of Oebalus and the grandson of Perieres. In a recently discovered fragment of the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Griechische Dichterfragmente, i., Epische und elegische Fragmente, bearbeitet von W. Schubart und U. von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff (Berlin, 1907), p. 30, line 38 (Berliner Klassikertexte 1)</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. ii.581</bibl>. According to the Scholiasts on Euripides and Homer, Icarius joined Hippocoon in driving his brother Tyndareus out of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Od. xv.16</bibl>, the wife of Icarius was Dorodoche, daughter of Ortilochus; but he adds that according to Pherecydes she was Asterodia, daughter of Eurypylus.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.20.10">Paus. 3.20.10ff.</bibl> According to the former of these passages, Ulysses won her hand in a footrace. As to races for brides, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. Epit. E.2.5">Apollod. E.2.5</bibl>; and note on

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 27, 64, 119ff., 163 (First Vatican Mythographer 78, 204; Second Vatican Mythographer 132; Third Vatican Mythographer 3.6)</bibl>. As the fruit of her intercourse with the swan, Leda is said to have laid an egg, which in the time of Pausanias was still to be seen hanging by ribbons from the roof of the temple of Hilaira and Phoebe at
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.16.1">Paus. 3.16.1</bibl>. According to one account (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">First Vatican Mythographer 78</bibl>), Castor, Pollux, and Helen all emerged from a single egg; according to another account (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">First Vatican Mythographer 204</bibl>), Leda laid two eggs, one of which produced Castor and Pollux, and the other Clytaemnestra and Helen. In heaven the twins Castor and Pollux had each, if we may believe Lucian, half an egg on or above his head in token of the way in which he had been hatched. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Lucian, Dial. Deorum xxvi.1</bibl>. For the distinction between Pollux and Castor, the former being regarded as the son of Zeus and the latter as the son of Tyndareus, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. N. 10">Pind. N. 10.79(149)ff.</bibl> According to Hesiod, both Pollux and Castor were sons of Zeus. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 88</bibl> (who may have followed Apollodorus);
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Ast. ii.8</bibl>. According to Eratosthenes and the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Callimachus, Hymn to Artemis, 232</bibl>, the meeting between Zeus and Nemesis, in the shape respectively of a swan and a goose, took place at Rhamnus in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 79</bibl>. The story was told by the historian Hellanicus (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. iii.144</bibl>), and in part by the poet Alcman (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Griechische Dichterfragmente</title>, i., <title>Epische und elegische Fragmente</title>, bearbeitet von W. Schubart und U. von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff (Berlin, 1907), pp. 28ff. (<title>Berliner Klassikertexte</title> 1)</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hesiod, in <title>Epische und elegische Fragmente</title>, ed. W. Schubart und U. von Wilamowitz-Moellendorff, p. 33</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.20.9">Paus. 3.20.9</bibl> the suitors took the oath standing on the severed pieces of a horse. As to the custom of standing on the pieces of a sacrificial victim or passing between them at the making of solemn covenants, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Folk-Lore in the Old Testament</title>, i.392ff.</bibl>
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 3.174">Hom. Il. 3.174ff.</bibl>) that Helen had only one child, her daughter Hermione. But according to Hesiod, whose verses are quoted by the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Soph. El. 539</bibl>, Helen afterwards bore a son Nicostratus to Menelaus. Compare

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Od. iv.11</bibl>, who tells us further that according to more recent writers Helen had a son Corythus or Helenus by Alexander (Paris). According to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Dictys Cretensis v.5</bibl>, Helen had three sons by Alexander, namely, Bunomus, Corythus, and Idaeus, who were accidentally killed at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. iii.175</bibl>, says that the Lacedaemonians worshipped two sons of Helen, to wit, Nicostratus and Aethiolas. He further mentions, on the authority of Ariaethus, that Helen had by Menelaus a son Maraphius, from whom the Persian family of the Maraphions was descended. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Dindorf's edition of the Scholiast on the Iliad vol. i. pp. 147ff., vol. iii. p. 171</bibl>. According to one account, Helen had a daughter by Theseus before she was married to Menelaus; this daughter was Iphigenia; Helen entrusted her to her sister Clytaemnestra, who reared the child and passed her off on her husband Agamemnon as her own offspring. This account of the parentage of Iphigenia was supported by the authority of Stesichorus and other poets. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ant. Lib. 27</bibl>. Sophocles represents Menelaus as having two children before he sailed for

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.10.3">Apollod. 3.10.3</bibl>). They invited to their wedding Castor and Pollux, who were cousins both to the bridegrooms and the brides, since Tyndareus, the human father of Castor and Pollux (see above,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.10.7">Apollod. 3.10.7</bibl>), was a brother of Aphareus and Leucippus (see above,

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.10.3">Apollod. 3.10.3</bibl>). But at the wedding Castor and Pollux carried off the brides, and being pursued by the bridegrooms, Idas and Lynceus, they turned on their pursuers. In the fight which ensued, Castor and Lynceus were slain, and Idas was killed by Zeus with a thunderbolt. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 27 (First Vatican Mythographer 77)</bibl>. According to Apollodorus, however, the fight between the cousins was occasioned by a quarrel arising over the division of some cattle which they had lifted from

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. N. 10">Pind. N. 10.60(112)ff.</bibl>) he speaks only of anger about cattle as the motive that led Idas to attack Castor. The rape of the daughters of Leucippus by Castor and Pollux was a favourite subject in art. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 4.31.9">Paus. 4.31.9</bibl>. The names of the damsels, as we learn from Apollodorus, were Phoebe and Hilaira. Compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.16.1">Paus. 3.16.1</bibl>. From an obscure gloss of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hesychius, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">πωλία</foreign> </bibl>, we may perhaps infer that these maiden priestesses, like the goddesses, were two in number, and that they were called “the colts of the Leucippides.” Further, since the name of Leucippus, the legendary father of the goddesses, means simply “White Horse,” it is tempting to suppose that the Leucippides, like their priestesses, were spoken of and perhaps conceived as white horses. More than that, Castor and Pollux, who carried off these white-horse maidens, if we may call them so, were not only constantly associated with horses, but were themselves called White Horses (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. P. 1">Pind. P. 1.66(126)</bibl> and “White Colts of Zeus” by Euripides in a fragment of his lost play the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">A. B. Cook, <title>Zeus</title>, i.442</bibl>. These coincidences can hardly be accidental. They point to the worship of a pair of brother deities conceived as white horses, and married to a pair of sister deities conceived as white mares, who were served by a pair of maiden priestesses called White Colts, assisted apparently by a boy priest or priests; for a Laconian inscription describes a certain youthful Marcus Aurelius Zeuxippus as “priest of the Leucippides and neatherd (?
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">P. Cauer, <title>Delectus Inscriptionum Graecarum propter dialectum memorabilium</title>, p. 17, No. 36</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">H. Collitz und F. Bechtel, <title>Sammlung der griechischen DialektInschriften</title>, iii.2, pp. 40ff., No. 4499</bibl>.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. p. 120 (Second Vatican Mythographer 132)</bibl>. The last of these writers explains the myth to mean that when the star of the one twin is setting, the star of the other is rising. It has been plausibly argued that in one of their aspects the twins were identified with the Morning and Evening Stars respectively, the immortal twin (Pollux) being conceived as the Morning Star, which is seen at dawn rising up in the sky till it is lost in the light of heaven, while the mortal twin (Castor) was identified with the Evening Star, which is seen at dusk sinking into its earthy bed. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> Rendel Harris, <title>The Dioscuri in the Christian Legends</title> (London, 1903), pp. 11ff.</bibl> It would seem that this view of the Spartan twins was favoured by the Spartans themselves, for after their great naval victory of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Cicero, De divinatione i.34.75, ii.32.68</bibl>. The same interpretation of the twins would accord well with their white horses (see the preceding note), on which the starry brethren might be thought to ride through the blue sky.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Ast. ii.4</bibl>. A different turn is given to the story by Homer, who represents the lovers meeting in a thrice-ploughed field (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 5.125">Hom. Od. 5.125-128</bibl>). To the same effect
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hes. Th. 969">Hes. Th. 969-974</bibl> says that the thrice-ploughed field where they met was in a fertile district of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Od. v.125</bibl>, attempts to rationalize the myth by saying that Iasion was the only man who preserved seed-corn after the deluge.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 20.215">Hom. Il. 20.215ff.</bibl> According to one account he was driven from
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Lycophron, Cassandra 72ff., with the scholia of Tzetzes</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. xx.215</bibl>. As to his marriage with Batia, daughter of Teucer, and his succession to the kingdom, compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Stephanus Byzantius, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Δάρδανες</foreign> </bibl>, Batia, the wife of Dardanus, was a daughter of Tros, not of Teucer.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 29</bibl>. As to Erichthonius, son of Dardanus, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Ant. Rom. i.50.3)</bibl> the names of the two sons whom Dardanus had by his wife Batia were Erichthonius and Zacynthus.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 20.230">Hom. Il. 20.230</bibl>, who does not mention the mother of Tros. She is named Astyoche, daughter of Simoeis, by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Diod. 4.75.3</bibl>. The name of the wife of Tros is not mentioned by Homer and Diodorus. She is called Callirrhoe, daughter of Scamander, by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholia Graeca in Homeri Iliadem Townleyana, ed. E. Maass, vol. ii. p. 321</bibl>.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 29</bibl>. The site of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Dionysius of Halicarnassus, Ant. Rom. i.68ff., ii.66.5</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Clement of Alexandria, Protrept. iv.47, p. 42, ed. Potter</bibl>;
