<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. 16.173-178</bibl>). Hence it is probable that here, as in so many places, Apollodorus followed Pherecydes. According to Staphylus, in the third book of his work on

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. 16.173-178</bibl>). A little later on (Apollod. 3.13.4) Apollodorus says that Peleus himself married Polydora, daughter of Perieres, and that she had a son Menesthius by the river Sperchius, though the child was nominally fathered on Peleus. In this latter passage Apollodorus seems to have fallen into confusion in describing Polydora as the wife of Peleus, though in the present passage he had correctly described her as his daughter. Compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hofer, in W. H. Roscher, <title>Lexikon der griech. und röm. Mythologie</title>, iii.2641ff.</bibl>

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 175 (vol. i. p. 447, ed. Muller)</bibl>. The Scholiast on Aristophanes, calls the slain man Eurytus, not Eurytion. Antoninus Liberalis and Tzetzes describe him as Eurytion, son of Irus, not of Actor. They do not mention the hunt of the Calydonian boar in particular, but speak of a boar-hunt or a hunt in general.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. N. 5">Pind. N. 5.25(46)ff.</bibl> It is told more explicitly by the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Ap. Rhod., Argon. i.224</bibl>. But the fullest and clearest version of the tale is given by Apollodorus in the present passage. Pindar calls the wicked wife Hippolyta or Hippolyta Cretheis, that is, Hippolyta daughter of Cretheus. His Scholiast calls her Cretheis; the Scholiast on Apollonius Rhodius, calls her Cretheis or Hippolyte; and the Scholiast on Aristophanes, calls her first Hippolyte and afterwards Astydamia. The sword of Peleus, which his faithless host hid in the cows' dung while the hero lay sleeping in the wood, was a magic sword wrought by the divine smith Hephaestus and bestowed on Peleus by the pitying gods as a reward for his chastity. With this wondrous brand the chaste hero, like a mediaeval knight, was everywhere victorious in the fight and successful in the chase. Compare
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Zenobius, Cent. v.20</bibl>. The episode of the hiding of the sword was told by Hesiod, some of whose verses on the subject are quoted by the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Pind. N. 4.59(95)</bibl>. The whole story of the adventures of Peleus in the house of Acastus and in the forest reads like a fairy tale, and we can hardly doubt that it contains elements of genuine folklore. These are well brought out by W. Mannhardt in his study of the story. See his
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">W. Mannhardt, <title>Antike Wald- und Feldkulte</title> (Berlin, 1877), pp. 49ff.</bibl>
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">W. Mannhardt, <title>Antike Wald- und Feldkulte</title>, pp. 53ff.</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild</title>, ii.269</bibl>.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 65, 142ff. (First Vatican Mythographer 207, 208; Second Vatican Mythographer 205)</bibl>.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 11.217">Ov. Met. 11.217ff.</bibl>, who attributes the prophecy to Proteus. The present passage of Apollodorus is quoted, with the author's name, by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Ast. ii.15</bibl>. According to Hyginus, Zeus released Prometheus from his fetters in gratitude for the warning which the sage had given him not to wed Thetis.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ap. Rhod., Argon. iv.790-798</bibl>, a passage which Apollodorus seems here to have had in mind.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 175, 178 (vol. i. pp. 446, 457, ed. Muller)</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 11.235">Ov. Met. 11.235ff.</bibl> She is said to have changed into fire, water, wind, a tree, a bird, a tiger, a lion, a serpent, and a cuttlefish. It was when she had assumed the form of a cuttlefish (sepia) that Peleus at last succeeded in seizing her and holding her fast (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 175, 178 (vol. i. pp. 446, 457, ed. Muller)</bibl>). With the transformations which Thetis underwent in order to escape from the arms of her lover we may compare the transformations which her father Nereus underwent in order to escape from Herakles (above,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 2.5.11">Apollod. 2.5.11</bibl>), the transformations which the river-god Achelous underwent in his tussle with the same doughty hero (above,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 2.7.5">Apollod. 2.7.5</bibl>, note), and the transformations which the sea-god Proteus underwent in order to give the slip to Menelaus (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 4.354">Hom. Od. 4.354ff.</bibl>). All these stories were appropriately told of water-spirits, their mutability reflecting as it were the instability of the fickle, inconstant element of which they were born. The place where Peleus caught and mastered his sea-bride was believed to be the southeastern headland of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hdt. 7.191">Hdt. 7.191</bibl>). See further, Frazer's Appendix to Apollodorus, “The Marriage of Peleus and Thetis.”
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. P. 3">Pind. P. 3.89(159)ff.</bibl> Catullus describes the Fates singing on the same occasion, and he has recorded their magic song (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 16.140">Hom. Il. 16.140-144</bibl>, with the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. 16.140</bibl>, according to whom Chiron felled the ash-tree for the shaft, while Athena polished it, and Hephaestus wrought (the blade). For this account the Scholiast refers to the author of the epic

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 178 (vol. i. p. 458, ed. Muller)</bibl>. According to another legend, Thetis bore seven sons, of whom Achilles was the seventh; she destroyed the first six by throwing them into the fire or into a kettle of boiling water to see whether they were mortal or to make them immortal by consuming the merely mortal portion of their frame; and the seventh son, Achilles, would have perished in like manner, if his father Peleus had not snatched him from the fire at the moment when as yet only his anklebone was burnt. To supply this missing portion of his body, Peleus dug up the skeleton of the giant Damysus, the fleetest of all the giants, and, extracting from it the anklebone, fitted it neatly into the ankle of his little son Achilles, applying drugs which caused the new, or rather old, bone to coalesce perfectly with the rest. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ptolemy Hephaest., Nov. Hist. vi in Westermann's Mythographi Graeci, p. 195</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Aristoph. Cl. 1068, p. 443, ed. Fr. Dubner</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Ap. Rhod., Argon. iv.816</bibl>. A similar story is told of Demeter and the infant son of Celeus. See above,

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ap. Rhod., Argon. iv.875ff.</bibl>, who says that when Thetis was interrupted by Peleus in her effort to make Achilles immortal, she threw the infant screaming on the floor, and rushing out of the house plunged angrily into the sea, and never returned again. In the Iliad Homer represents Thetis dwelling with her old father Nereus and the sea-nymphs in the depths of the sea (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 14.83">Hom. Il. 14.83ff.</bibl>), while her forlorn husband dragged out a miserable and solitary old age in the halls (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 18.434">Hom. Il. 18.434ff.</bibl>). Thus the poet would seem to have been acquainted with the story of the quarrel and parting of the husband and wife, though he nowhere alludes to it or to the painful misunderstanding which led to their separation. In this, as in many other places, Homer passes over in silence features of popular tradition which he either rejected as incredible or deemed below the dignity of the epic. Yet if we are right in classing the story of Peleus and Thetis with the similar tales of the marriage of a man to a mermaid or other marine creature, the narrative probably always ended in the usual sad way by telling how, after living happily together for a time, the two at last quarrelled and parted for ever.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Il. xvi.37</bibl>. According to

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius (Achill. ii.382ff.)</bibl>, Chiron fed the youthful Achilles not on ordinary victuals, but on the flesh and marrows of lions. Philostratus says that his nourishment consisted of honeycombs and the marrows of fawns (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Philostratus, Her. xx.2</bibl>), while the author of the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Etymologicum Magnum, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Ἀχιλλεύς</foreign>, p. 181</bibl> says that he was nurtured on the marrows of deer. Compare

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Eustathius on Hom. Il. 1.1, p. 14</bibl>. The flesh and marrows of lions, wild boars, and bears were no doubt supposed to impart to the youthful hero who partook of them the strength and courage of these animals, while the marrows of fawns or deer may have been thought to ensure the fleetness of foot for which he was afterwards so conspicuous. It is thus that on the principle of sympathetic magic many races seek to acquire the qualities of certain animals by eating their flesh or drinking their blood; whereas they abstain from eating the flesh of other animals lest they should, by partaking of it, be infected with the undesirable qualities which these creatures are believed to possess. For example, in various African tribes men eat the hearts of lions in order to become lionhearted, while others will not eat the flesh of tortoises lest they should become slow-footed like these animals. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Spirits of the Corn and of the Wild</title>, ii.138ff.</bibl> On the same principle the ancients believed that men could acquire the art of divination by eating the hearts of ravens, moles, or hawks, because these creatures were supposed to be endowed with prophetic powers. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Pliny, Nat. Hist. xxx.19</bibl>. So Medea is said to have restored the aged Aeson to youth by infusing into his veins a decoction of the liver of a long-lived stag and of the head of a crow that had survived nine generations of men. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.13.3">Apollod. 3.13.3</bibl>. But it is probable that the cutting of the bad woman in pieces and marching between the pieces into the city was more than a simple act of vengeance; it may have been a solemn sacrifice or purification designed to ensure the safety of the army in the midst of a hostile people. In

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Plut. Quaest. Rom. 111</bibl>. A similar rite was observed at purifying a Macedonian army. A dog was cut in two: the head and fore part were placed on the right, the hinder part, with the entrails, was placed on the left, and the troops in arms marched between the pieces. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Quintus Curtius, De gestis Alexandri Magni x.9.28</bibl>. For more examples of similar rites, and an attempt to explain them, see

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>Folk-Lore in the Old Testament</title>, i.391ff.</bibl> To the instances there cited may be added another. When the Algerine pirates were at sea and in extreme danger, it was their custom to sacrifice a sheep, cut off its head, extract its entrails, and then throw them, together with the head, overboard; afterwards “with all the speed they can (without skinning) they cut the body in two parts by the middle, and then throw one part over the right side of the ship, and the other over the left, into the sea, as a kind of propitiation.” See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Joseph Pitts, <title>A true and faithful Account of the Religion and Manners of the Mohammetans</title> (Exon. 1704), p. 14</bibl>. As to the capture of Iolcus by Peleus, see

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Pind. N. 4">Pind. N. 4.54(89)ff.</bibl> In the former of these passages Pindar says that Peleus captured Iolcus single-handed; but the Scholiast on the passage affirms, on the authority of Pherecydes, that he was accompanied by Jason and the Tyndarids (Castor and Pollux). As this statement tallies with the account given by Apollodorus, we may surmise that here, as often elsewhere, our author followed Pherecydes. According to the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Ap. Rhod., Argon. i.224</bibl>, Peleus on his return to Iolcus put to death Acastus himself as well as his wicked wife.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ptolemy Hephaest., Nov. Hist. i. in Westermann's Mythographi Graeci, p. 183</bibl>.

Apollodorus apparently describes the infant Erichthonius in the chest as a purely human babe with a serpent coiled about him. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Ion 20">Eur. Ion 20ff.</bibl>, there were two such guardian serpents. But according to a common tradition Erichthonius was serpent-footed, that is, his legs ended in serpents. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 41, 87 (First Vatican Mythographer 128, Second Vatican Mythographer 37)</bibl>. Indeed, in one passage (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Astronom. ii.13</bibl>) Hyginus affirms that Erichthonius was born a serpent, and that when the box was opened and the maidens saw the serpent in it, they went mad and threw themselves from the acropolis, while the serpent took refuge under the shield of Athena and was reared by the goddess. This view of the identity of Erichthonius with the serpent was recognized, if not accepted, by Pausanias; for in describing the famous statue of the Virgin Athena on the acropolis of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.24.7">Paus. 1.24.7</bibl>). The sacred serpent which lived in the Erechtheum on the acropolis of
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Aristoph. Lys. 758">Aristoph. Lys. 758ff.</bibl>, with the Scholiast;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Eustathius on Hom. Od. i.357, p. 1422, lines 7ff.</bibl> According to some, there were two such sacred serpents in the Erechtheum (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hesychius, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">οἰκουρὸν ὄφιν</foreign> </bibl>). When we remember that Cecrops, the ancestor of Erichthonius, was said, like his descendant, to be half-man, half-serpent (above,
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 3.14.1">Apollod. 3.14.1</bibl>), we may conjecture that the old kings of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>The Dying God</title>, pp. 86ff.</bibl>; and Frazer on Paus. 1.18.2 (vol. ii. pp. 168ff.). See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Eur. Ion 1426">Eur. Ion 1426-1431</bibl>. Erechtheus and Erichthonius may have been originally identical. See Scholiast on
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">C. F. Clinton, <title>Fasti Hellenici</title>, vol. i. p. 61 note (n)</bibl>.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Fulgentius, Mytholog. ii.14</bibl>. According to some, he invented the chariot for the purpose of concealing his serpent feet. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Clement of Alexandria, Protrept. iii.45, p. 39, ed. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.13.1">Paus. 3.13.1</bibl>), the tomb of Hyacinth under the image of Apollo at Amyclae (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 3.19.3">Paus. 3.19.3</bibl>), and the grave of Arcas in a temple of Hera at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Marmor Parium 22, 30</bibl>). Eusebius also recognizes Pandion the Second, but makes him a son of Erechtheus instead of a son of Cecrops the Second (

The Athenians celebrated a curious festival of swinging, which was supposed to be an expiation for the death of Erigone, who had hanged herself on the same tree at the foot of which she had discovered the dead body of her father Icarius (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Festus, s.v. “<foreign xml:lang="lat">Oscillantes</foreign>,” p. 194, ed. C. O. Muller</bibl>. Compare

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. Epit. E.6.25">Apollod. E.6.25</bibl> with the note). Sophocles wrote a play
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <title>The Fragments of Sophocles</title>, ed. A. C. Pearson, vol. i. pp. 173ff.</bibl> The home of Icarius was at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Statius, Theb. xi.644-647</bibl> we infer that the place was in the woods of Marathon, and in accordance with this description the site has been discovered in a beautiful wooded dell at the northern foot of the forest-clad slopes of Mount Pentelicus. The place is still appropriately named Dionysos. A rugged precipitous path leads down a wild romantic ravine from the deserted village of Rapentosa to the plain of Marathon situated at a great depth below. Among the inscriptions found on the spot several refer to the worship of Dionysus. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.41.8">Paus. 1.41.8ff.</bibl>). But no one who has seen the grey ruined walls and towers of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 6.675">Ov. Met. 6.675ff.</bibl> According to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 6.675">Ov. Met. 6.675ff.</bibl> Erechtheus had four sons and four daughters.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Harpocration, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Βούτης</foreign> </bibl>, who tells us that the families of the Butads and Eteobutads traced their origin to this Butes. There was an altar dedicated to him as to a hero in the Erechtheum on the acropolis of

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hdt. 7.189">Hdt. 7.189</bibl>), assumes in the present passage. This inference is confirmed by an express statement of the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Ap. Rhod., Argon. i.212</bibl> that Cecrops was the father of Orithyia. As to the vase-painting in question, see

Of these writers, Tzetzes closely follows Apollodorus, whom he cites by name. They are the only two authors who mention the intrigue of Procris with Pteleus and the bribe of the golden crown. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Hom. Od. xi.321</bibl>, who gives an abstract of the narrative. In it the test of his wife's chastity is made by Cephalus himself in disguise; nothing is said of the flight of the abashed Procris to Minos, and nothing of the love of Dawn (Aurora) for Cephalus, which in several of the versions figures conspicuously, since it is the jealous goddess who suggests to her human lover the idea of tempting his wife to her fall. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 2.7.1">Apollod. 2.7.1</bibl>. The animal's name was Laelaps (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 189</bibl>, both the dog and the dart which could never miss were bestowed on Procris by Artemis (Diana). Sophocles wrote a tragedy

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ant. Lib. 41</bibl>. According to him, the animals which Minos discharged from his body were snakes, scorpions, and millipeds.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Chiliades i.552</bibl>. After the homicide of his wife, Cephalus is said to have dwelt as an exile in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. A. 3.209">Serv. Verg. A. 3.209</bibl>. According to Hyginus, their wings were attached to their feet, and their hair was sky-blue. Elsewhere (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 19</bibl>) he describes them with wings on their heads as well as on their feet. Ovid says that they were twins, and that they did not develop wings until their beards began to grow; according to him, the pinions sprouted from their sides in the usual way.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ap. Rhod., Argon. i.1298-1308</bibl>, who tells us that when Zetes and Calais were returning from the funeral games of Pelias, Herakles killed them in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Apollod. 1.9.21">Apollod. 1.9.21</bibl>. The story of Phineus and his sons is related by the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Sophocles (Antigone, 981)</bibl>, referring to the present passage of Apollodorus as his authority. The tale was told by the ancients with many variations, some of which are noticed by the

Ant. 969ff.</bibl>, it was not their father Phineus, but their cruel stepmother, who blinded the two young men, using her shuttle as a dagger. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Eur. Alc. 1</bibl>. Both Aeschylus and Sophocles composed tragedies entitled

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 7.1.5">Paus. 7.1.5</bibl>); and with this account

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 46</bibl>, Zeus killed Erechtheus with a thunderbolt at the request of Poseidon, who was enraged at the Athenians for killing his son Eumolpus.

See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Ast. ii.5</bibl>. The picturesque story was painted by Micon in the sanctuary of Theseus at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.27.10">Paus. 1.27.10</bibl> mentions the killing of Androgeus by the Marathonian bull. According to

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Lactantius Placidus on Statius, Theb. i.333, vii.261</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 238</bibl> (who seems to mention only one daughter; but the passage is corrupt);

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Harpocration, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Ὑακινθίδες</foreign> </bibl>, who says that the daughters of Hyacinth the Lacedaemonian were known as the Hyacinthides. The name of one of the daughters of Hyacinth is said to have been Lusia (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Cicero, De natura deorum iii.19.50</bibl>. So, too, in
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 13.685">Ov. Met. 13.685-699</bibl>. The frequency of such legends, among which the traditional sacrifice of Iphigenia at

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Plat. Ion 121a</bibl>, both of whom name the father and mother of Daedalus in agreement with Apollodorus. The father of Daedalus is called Eupalamus also by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Soph. OC 472</bibl>); and this tradition as to the father of Daedalus is supported by

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 7.4.5">Paus. 7.4.5</bibl> “that Daedalus came of the royal house of

Toepffer, <title>Attische Genealogie</title>, pp. 165ff.</bibl> Through the clouds of fable which gathered round his life and adventures we may dimly discern the figure of a vagabond artist as versatile as Leonardo da Vinci and as unscrupulous as Benvenuto Cellini.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas and Photius, Lexicon, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Πέρδικος ἱερόν</foreign> </bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Serv. G. 1.143">Serv. Verg. G. 1.143</bibl> and
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Isidore, Orig. xix.19.9</bibl>. The name of the murdered nephew is commonly given as Talos, but according to
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas and Photius, Lexicon, s.v. <foreign xml:lang="grc">Πέρδικος ἱερόν;</foreign> </bibl> it was Calos. On the other hand Sophocles, in his lost play

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas and Photius,ll.cc.</bibl>) called him Perdix, that is, Partridge; and this name is accepted by Ovid, Hyginus, Servius, and Isidore. But according to a different tradition, here followed by Apollodorus, Perdix (“Partridge”) was the name, not of the murdered nephew, but of his mother, the sister of Daedalus, who hanged herself in grief at the death of her son; the Athenians worshipped her and dedicated a sanctuary to her beside the acropolis (so Apostolius,

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Suidas and Photius, ll.cc.</bibl>). The grave of Talos or Calos was shown near the theatre, at the foot of the acropolis, probably on the spot where he was supposed to have fallen from the battlements (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 1.21.4">Paus. 1.21.4</bibl>). The trial of Daedalus before the Areopagus is mentioned by Diodorus Siculus and the Scholiast on Euripides l.c..
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Chiliades i.494ff.</bibl> Latin writers held that the invention was suggested to him by the backbone of a fish. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Isidore, Orig. xix.19.9</bibl>. According to these Latin writers, the ingenious artist invented the compass also. As to Talos or Perdix and his mechanical inventions, see
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Lucian, Jupiter Tragoedus 21, pp. 64ff., ed. H. Rabe</bibl>;
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Pind. I., Arg. p. 514, ed. Boeckh</bibl>;

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 38</bibl>. Bacchylides, the Scholiast on Pindar, and Hyginus call Sinis a son of Poseidon (Neptune). The ancients are not agreed as to the exact mode in which the ruffian Sinis despatched his victims. According to Diodorus, Pausanias, and the Scholiast on Pindar he bent two pine-trees to the ground, tied the extremities of his victim to both trees, and then let the trees go, which, springing up and separating, tore the wretch's body in two. This atrocious form of murder was at a later time actually employed by the emperor Aurelian in a military execution. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Vopiscus, Aurelian, 7.4</bibl>. A Ruthenian pirate, named Botho, is said to have put men to death in similar fashion. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Saxo Grammaticus, Historia Danica, bk. vii. vol. i. pp. 353ff., ed. P. E. Müller</bibl>. According to Hyginus, Sinis, with the help of his victim, dragged down a pine-tree to the earth; then, when the man was struggling to keep the tree down, Sinis released it, and in the rebound the man was tossed up into the air and killed by falling heavily to the ground. Apollodorus seems to have contemplated a similar mode of death, except that he does not mention the cooperation of Sinis in bending the tree to the earth. According to the
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Marmor Parium 35ff.</bibl>) it was not on his journey from

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Plut. Thes. 8.2">Plut. Thes. 8.2</bibl> that when Theseus had killed Sinis, the daughter of the dead man, by name Perigune, fled and hid herself in a bed of asparagus; that she bore a son Melanippus to Theseus, and that Melanippus had a son Ioxus, whose descendants, the Ioxids, both men and women, revered and honoured asparagus and would not burn it, because asparagus had once sheltered their ancestress. This hereditary respect shown by all the members of a family or clan for a particular species of plant is reminiscent of totemism, though it is not necessarily a proof of it.

Plutarch notices a rationalistic version of the story, which converted the sow Phaea into a female robber of that name. No ancient writer but Apollodorus mentions the old woman Phaea who nursed the sow, but she appears on vase paintings which represent the slaughter of the sow by Theseus. See
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Baumeister, <title>Denkmäler des klassischen Altertums</title>, iii. pp. 1787ff., 1789, fig. 1873</bibl>;

Curiously enough, the Second Vatican Mythographer attributes the despatching of Sciron, not to Theseus, but to the artist Daedalus. The Megarians, as we learn from Plutarch, indignantly denied the defamatory reports current as to the character and pursuits of their neighbour Sciron, whom they represented as a most respectable man, the foe of robbers, the friend of the virtuous, and connected by marriage with families of the highest quality; but their efforts to whitewash the blackguard appear to have been attended with little success. The Scironian Rocks, to which Sciron was supposed to have given his name, are a line of lofty cliffs rising sheer from the sea; a narrow, crumbling ledge about half way up their face afforded a perilous foothold, from which the adventurous traveller looked down with horror on the foam of the breakers far below. The dangers of the path were obviated about the middle of the nineteenth century by the construction of a road and railway along the coast. See Frazer's note on Paus. 1.44.6 (vol. ii. pp. 546ff. ).

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Scholiast on Lucian, l.c.</bibl> says that it was near Eleutherae, but he is probably in error; for if the place were near Eleutherae, it must have been on the road from

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 38</bibl>. Ancient authorities are not agreed as to the name of this malefactor. Apollodorus and Plutarch call him Damastes; but Apollodorus says that some people called him Polypemon, and this latter name is supported by Pausanias, who adds that he was surnamed Procrustes. Ovid in two passages (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 7.438">Ov. Met. 7.438, Her. ii. 69</bibl>) calls him simply Procrustes, but in a third passage (

The promised land was the White Isle mentioned by Apollodorus. It is described as a wooded island off the mouth of the Danube. In it there was a temple of Achilles with an image of him; and there the hero was said to dwell immortal with Helen for his wife and his friends Patroclus and Antilochus for his companions. There he chanted the verses of Homer, and mariners who sailed near the island could hear the song wafted clearly across the water; while such as put in to the shore or anchored off the coast, heard the trampling of horses, the shouts of warriors, and the clash of arms. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 174</bibl>. According to the

Rhod., Argon. iv.815</bibl>, the first to affirm that Achilles married Medea in the Elysian Fields was the poet Ibycus, and the tale was afterwards repeated by Simonides. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Posthomerica iv.405ff., 436ff.</bibl>); and he seems to have described Eumelus as the winner of the chariot-race (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Quintus Smyrnaeus, Posthomerica iv.500ff.</bibl>), but the conclusion of the race is lost through a gap in the text.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Aristot. Poet. 1459b.4">Aristot. Poet. 1459b 4ff.</bibl>. The contest between Ajax and Ulysses for the arms of Achilles was also related in the

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ap. Rhod., Argon. iv.898ff.</bibl>) describes the Sirens as partly virgins and partly birds. Aelian tells us (

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Ael., Nat. Anim. xvii.23</bibl>) that poets and painters represented them as winged maidens with the feet of birds. Ovid says that the Sirens had the feet and feathers of birds, but the faces of virgins; and he asks why these daughters of Achelous, as he calls them, had this hybrid form. Perhaps, he thinks, it was because they had been playing with Persephone when gloomy Dis carried her off, and they had begged the gods to grant them wings, that they might search for their lost playmate over seas as well as land. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Ov. Met. 5.552">Ov. Met. 5.552-562</bibl>. <bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hyginus, Fab. 125, 141</bibl>. Another story was that they were maidens whom Aphrodite turned into birds because they chose to remain unmarried. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Eustathius on Hom. Od. 12.47, p. 1709</bibl>. It is said that they once vied with the Muses in singing, and that the Muses, being victorious, plucked off the Siren's feathers and made crowns out of them for themselves (
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Paus. 9.34.3">Paus. 9.34.3</bibl>). In ancient art, as in literature, the Sirens are commonly represented as women above and birds below. See

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 12.89">Hom. Od. 12. 89ff.</bibl>). The suspicion that Penelope was unfaithful to her husband has no support in Homer.

cits: <cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote> <milestone unit="para"/>And Theseus allied himself with Pirithous,<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">This passage concerning the fight of Theseus with the centaurs at the marriage of Pirithous does not occur in our text of Apollodorus, but is conjecturally restored to it from <bibl>Zenobius, Cent. v.33</bibl>, or rather from his interpolator, who frequently quotes passages of Apollodorus without acknowledgment. The restoration was first proposed by Professor C. Robert before the discovery of the Epitome; and it is adopted by R. Wagner in his edition of Apollodorus. See <bibl>C. Robert, <title>De Apollodori Bibliotheca</title>, pp. 49ff.</bibl>; <bibl>R. Wagner, <title>Epitoma Vaticana ex Apollodori Bibliotheca</title>, p. 147</bibl>. As Pirithous was a son of Ixion (see above, <bibl n="Apollod. 1.8.2">Apollod. 1.8.2</bibl>), the account of his marriage would follow naturally after the recital of his father's crime and punishment. As to the wedding of Pirithous, see further <bibl>Diod. 4.70.3</bibl>; <bibl n="Plut. Thes. 30">Plut. Thes. 30</bibl>; <bibl n="Paus. 5.10.8">Paus. 5.10.8</bibl>; <bibl>Scholiast on Hom. Od. xxi.295</bibl>; <bibl>Hyginus, Fab. 33</bibl>; <bibl n="Ov. Met. 12.210">Ov. Met. 12.210-535</bibl>; <bibl n="Serv. A. 7.304">Serv. Verg. A. 7.304</bibl>; <bibl>Scriptores rerum mythicarum Latini, ed. Bode, i. pp. 51, 111 (First Vatican Mythographer 162; Second Vatican Mythographer 108)</bibl>. The wife of Pirithous is called Deidamia by Plutarch, but Hippodamia by Diodorus Siculus, Hyginus, and the Second Vatican Mythographer, as well as by <bibl n="Hom. Il. 2.742">Hom. Il. 2.742</bibl>. Ovid calls her Hippodame. The scene of the battle of the Lapiths with the centaurs at the wedding of Pirithous was sculptured in the western gable of the temple of Zeus at <name type="place" key="perseus,Olympia">Olympia</name>; all the sculptures were discovered, in a more or less fragmentary state, by the Germans in their excavations of the sanctuary, and they are now exhibited in the museum at <name type="place" key="perseus,Olympia">Olympia</name>. See <bibl n="Paus. 5.10.8">Paus. 5.10.8</bibl>, with my commentary ( <bibl>Frazer, Paus. vol. iii. pp. 516ff.</bibl>).</note> when he engaged in war against the centaurs. For when <pb n="151"/>Pirithous wooed Hippodamia, he feasted the centaurs because they were her kinsmen. But being unaccustomed to wine, they made themselves drunk by swilling it greedily, and when the bride was brought in, they attempted to violate her. But Pirithous, fully armed, with Theseus, joined battle with them, and Theseus killed many of them. </quote> <bibl>Zenobius, Cent. v. 33.</bibl> </cit>

Guneus left his own ships, and having come to the Cinyps river in <name type="place" key="tgn,1000172">Libya</name> he dwelt there.<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">According to another account, Guneus was drowned at sea. See <bibl n="Aristot. Pepl. 32">Aristot. Peplos 32(37), in Bergk's <title>Poetae Lyrici Graeci</title>, ii.654</bibl>.</note> But Meges and Prothous, with many others, were cast away at Caphereus in <name type="place" key="tgn,7002677">Euboea</name> <note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">Epitaphs on these two drowned men are ascribed to <bibl n="Aristot. Pepl. 25">Aristot. Peplos 25(19)</bibl> and <bibl n="Aristot. Pepl. 28">28(38)</bibl>. See <bibl> <title>Bergk's Poetae Lyrici Graeci</title>, ii.653, 654</bibl>. Meges was leader of the Dulichians, and Prothous was leader of the Magnesians. See <bibl n="Apollod. Epit. E.3.12">Apollod. E.3.12</bibl> and <bibl n="Apollod. Epit. E.14">Apollod. E.14</bibl>.</note>... and when Prothous was shipwrecked at Caphereus, the Magnesians with him drifted to <name type="place" key="tgn,7012056">Crete</name> and settled there. </quote> <bibl>Tzetzes, Scholia on Lycophron, 902</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote> <milestone unit="para"/>After the sack of <name type="place" key="perseus,Troy">Ilium</name>,<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">This paragraph is quoted from <bibl>Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 911</bibl>.</note> Menestheus, Phidippus and Antiphus, and the people of Elephenor, and Philoctetes sailed together as far as Mimas. Then Menestheus went to <name type="place" key="perseus,Melos City">Melos</name> and reigned as king, because the king there, Polyanax, had died. And Antiphus the son of Thessalus went to the Pelasgians, and having taken possession of the country he called it <name type="place" key="tgn,7001399">Thessaly</name>.<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">Compare <bibl n="Strab. 9.5.23">Strab. 9.5.23</bibl>.</note> Phidippus with the Coans was driven first to <name type="place" key="tgn,7010719">Andros</name>, and then to <name type="place" key="tgn,1000112">Cyprus</name>, where he settled. Elephenor died in <name type="place" key="perseus,Troy">Troy</name>,<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">Elephenor was killed in battle by Agenor. See <bibl n="Hom. Il. 4.463">Hom. Il. 4.463-472</bibl>. Compare <bibl n="Aristot. Pepl. 33">Aristot. Peplos 33(4), in Bergk's <title>Poetae Lyrici Graeci</title>, ii.654</bibl>.</note> but his people were cast away in the Ionian gulf and inhabited <name type="place" key="perseus,Apollonia">Apollonia</name> in <name type="place" key="tgn,7002705">Epirus</name>. And the people of Tlepolemus touched <pb n="261"/>at <name type="place" key="tgn,7012056">Crete</name>; then they were driven out of their course by winds and settled in the Iberian islands. ...The people of Protesilaus were cast away on <name type="place" key="perseus,Pellene">Pellene</name> near the plain of Canastrum.<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">Canastrum, or Canastra, is the extreme southern cape of the peninsula of <name type="place" key="perseus,Pallene">Pallene</name> (<name type="place" key="perseus,Pellene">Pellene</name>) in <name type="place" key="tgn,7006667">Macedonia</name>. See <bibl n="Hdt. 7.123">Hdt. 7.123</bibl>; <bibl>Ap. Rhod., Argon. i.599, with the Scholiast</bibl>; <bibl n="Strab. 7.fragments.25">Strab. 7 Fr. 25</bibl>; <bibl>Apostolius, Cent. ii.20</bibl>; <bibl>Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 526</bibl>; <bibl>Livy xxx.45.15, xliv.11.3</bibl>.</note> And Philoctetes was driven to <name type="place" key="tgn,7003005">Campania</name> in <name type="place" key="tgn,1000080">Italy</name>, and after making war on the Lucanians, he settled in Crimissa, near <name type="place" key="perseus,Croton">Croton</name> and <name type="place" key="tgn,6005942">Thurium</name> <note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">It is said that in a sedition Philoctetes was driven from his city of <name type="place" key="perseus,Meliboea">Meliboea</name> in <name type="place" key="tgn,7001399">Thessaly</name> (<bibl n="Hom. Il. 2.717">Hom. Il. 2.717ff.</bibl>), and fled to southern <name type="place" key="tgn,1000080">Italy</name>, where he founded the cities of Petilia, Old Crimissa, and Chone, between <name type="place" key="perseus,Croton">Croton</name> and <name type="place" key="perseus,Thurii">Thurii</name>. See <bibl n="Strab. 6.1.3">Strab. 6.1.3</bibl>, who, after recording the foundation of Petilia and Old Crimissa by Philoctetes, proceeds as follows: “And Apollodorus, after mentioning Philoctetes in his <title>Book of the Ships</title>, says that some people relate how, on arriving in the country of <name type="place" key="perseus,Croton">Croton</name>, he founded Crimissa on the headland and above it the city of Chone, from which the Chonians hereabout took their name, and how men sent by him to <name type="place" key="tgn,7003122">Sicily</name> fortified Segesta near <name type="place" key="perseus,Eryx">Eryx</name> with the help of Aegestes the Trojan.” The book from which Strabo makes this quotation is not the <title>Library</title> of our author, but the <title>Catalogue of the Ships</title>, a work on the Homeric Catalogue by the Athenian grammarian Apollodorus. According to <bibl n="Strab. 8.3.6">Strab. 8.3.6</bibl>, Apollodorus borrowed most of his materials for this work from Demetrius of Scepsis. For the fragments of the work see <bibl>Heyne's Apollodorus (Second Edition, 1803), vol. i. pp. 417ff.</bibl>; <bibl>Fragmenta Historicorum Graecorum, ed. C. Müller, i.453ff.</bibl> </note>; and, his wanderings over, he founded a sanctuary of Apollo the Wanderer (<hi rend="ital">Alaios</hi>), to whom also he dedicated his bow, as Euphorion says.<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">Compare <bibl n="Aristot. Mir. 107">Aristot. Mir. 107(115)</bibl>: “It is said that Philoctetes is worshipped by the Sybarites; for on his return from <name type="place" key="perseus,Troy">Troy</name> he settled in the territory of <name type="place" key="perseus,Croton">Croton</name> at the place called Macalla, which they say is distant a hundred and twenty furlongs, and they relate that he dedicated the bow of Hercules in the sanctuary of the Halian Apollo. But they say that in the time of their sovereignty the people of <name type="place" key="perseus,Croton">Croton</name> fetched the bow from there and dedicated it in the sanctuary of Apollo in their country. It is said, too, that when he died he was buried beside the river <name type="place" key="perseus,Sybaris">Sybaris</name>; for he had gone to the help of the Rhodians under Tlepolemus, who had been carried out of their course to these regions and had engaged in battle with the barbarous inhabitants of that country.” This war with the barbarians is no doubt the “war on the Lucanians,” in which Apollodorus, or at all events, Tzetzes here tells us that Philoctetes engaged after his arrival in <name type="place" key="tgn,1000080">Italy</name>.</note> </quote> <bibl>Tzetzes, Scholia on Lycophron, 911</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote> <milestone unit="para"/>Navaethus is a river of <name type="place" key="tgn,1000080">Italy</name>.<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">This paragraph is quoted from <bibl>Tzetzes, Scholiast on Lycophron 921</bibl>.</note> It was called so, according to Apollodorus and the rest, because after the capture of <name type="place" key="perseus,Troy">Ilium</name> the daughters of Laomedon, the <pb n="263"/>sisters of Priam, to wit, Aethylla, Astyoche, and Medesicaste, with the other female captives, finding themselves in that part of <name type="place" key="tgn,1000080">Italy</name>, and dreading slavery in <name type="place" key="tgn,1000074">Greece</name>, set fire to the vessels; whence the river was called Navaethus and the women were called Nauprestides; and the Greeks who were with the women, having lost the vessels, settled there.<note anchored="true" resp="ed" place="unspecified">The same story is told by Strabo, who calls the river Neaethus (<bibl n="Strab. 6.1.12">Strab. 6.1.12</bibl>). Stephanus Byzantius agrees with Apollodorus in giving Navaethus (<foreign xml:lang="grc">Ναύαιθος</foreign>) as the form of the name. Apollodorus derives the name from <foreign xml:lang="grc">ναῦς</foreign>, “a ship,” and <foreign xml:lang="grc">αἴθω</foreign>, “to burn.” Virgil tells a similar tale of the founding of Segesta or, as he calls it, Acesta in <name type="place" key="tgn,7003122">Sicily</name>. See <bibl n="Verg. A. 5.604">Verg. A. 5.604-771</bibl>.</note> </quote> <bibl>Tzetzes, Scholia on Lycophron, 921</bibl> </cit>

Ἀπολλόδωρος δὲ καὶ οἱ λοιποὶ οὕτω φασί· Γουνεὺς εἰς Λιβύην λιπὼν τὰς ἑαυτοῦ ναῦς ἐλθὼν ἐπὶ Κίνυφα ποταμὸν κατοικεῖ. Μέγης δὲ καὶ Πρόθοος ἐν Εὐβοίᾳ περὶ τὸν Καφηρέα σὺν πολλοῖς ἑτέροις διαφθείρεται τοῦ δὲ Προθόου περὶ τὸν Καφηρέα ναυαγήσαντος, οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ Μάγνητες εἰς Κρήτην ῥιφέντες ᾤκησαν.

τζετζες, σξηολια ον λψξοπηρον, 902

μετὰ δὲ τὴν Ἰλίου πόρθησιν Μενεσθεὺς Φείδιππός τε καὶ Ἄντιφος καὶ οἱ Ἐλεφήνορος καὶ Φιλοκτήτης μέχρι Μίμαντος κοινῇ ἔπλευσαν. εἶτα Μενεσθεὺς μὲν εἰς Μῆλον ἐλθὼν βασιλεύει, τοῦ ἐκεῖ βασιλέως Πολυάνακτος τελευτήσαντος. Ἄντιφος δὲ ὁ Θεσσαλοῦ εἰς Πελασγοὺς ἐλθὼν καὶ τὴν χώραν κατασχὼν Θεσσαλίαν ἐκάλεσε. Φείδιππος δὲ μετὰ Κῴων ἐξωσθεὶς περὶ τὴν Ἄνδρον, εἶτα περὶ Κύπρον ἐκεῖ κατῴκησεν. Ἐλεφήνορος δὲ ἀποθανόντος ἐν Τροίᾳ, οἱ σὺν αὐτῷ ἐκριφέντες περὶ τὸν Ἰόνιον κόλπον Ἀπολλωνίαν ᾤκησαν τὴν ἐν Ἠπείρῳ. καὶ οἱ τοῦ Τληπολέμου προσίσχουσι Κρήτῃ, εἶτα ὑπʼ ἀνέμων ἐξωσθέντες περὶ τὰς Ἰβηρικὰς νήσους ᾤκησαν οἱ τοῦ Πρωτεσιλάου εἰς Πελλήνην ἀπερρίφησαν πλησίον πεδίου Κανάστρου. Φιλοκτήτης δὲ ἐξώσθη εἰς Ἰταλίαν πρὸς Καμπανοὺς καὶ πολεμήσας Λευκανοὺς πλησίον Κρότωνος καὶ Θουρίου Κρίμισσαν κατοικεῖ· καὶ παυθεὶς τῆς ἄλης Ἀλαίου Ἀπόλλωνος ἱερὸν κτίζει, ᾧ καὶ τὸ τόξον αὑτοῦ ἀνέθηκεν, ὥς φησιν Εὐφορίων.

Ναύαιθος ποταμός ἐστιν Ἰταλίας· ἐκλήθη δὲ οὕτω κατὰ μὲν Ἀπολλόδωρον καὶ τοὺς λοιπούς, ὅτι μετὰ τὴν Ἰλίου ἅλωσιν αἱ Λαομέδοντος θυγατέρες, Πριάμου δὲ ἀδελφαί, Αἴθυλλα Ἀστυόχη Μηδεσικάστη μετὰ τῶν λοιπῶν αἰχμαλωτίδων ἐκεῖσε γεγονυῖαι τῆς Ἰταλίας, εὐλαβούμεναι τὴν ἐν τῇ Ἑλλάδι δουλείαν τὰ σκάφη ἐνέπρησαν, ὅθεν ὁ ποταμὸς Ναύαιθος ἐκλήθη καὶ αἱ γυναῖκες Ναυπρήστιδες· οἱ δὲ σὺν αὐταῖς Ἕλληνες ἀπολέσαντες τὰ σκάφη ἐκεῖ κατῴκησανgt.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Hom. Od. unknown line</bibl>ταύτην εἶναι θυγατέρα Ἰνάχου γυναῖκα δὲ Ἀρέστορος τὰ ἔπη λέγει, ἃ δὴ Ἕλληνες καλοῦσιν Ἠοίας μεγάλας· ἀπὸ ταύτης οὖν γεγονέναι καὶ τὸ ὄνομα τῇ πόλει φασίν. ὃν δὲ προσποιοῦσιν Ἀκουσιλάῳ λόγον, Μυκηνέα υἱὸν εἶναι Σπάρτωνος, Σπάρτωνα δὲ Φορωνέως, οὐκ ἂν ἔγωγε ἀποδεξαίμην, διότι μηδὲ αὐτοὶ Λακεδαιμόνιοι. Λακεδαιμονίοις γὰρ Σπάρτης μὲν γυναικὸς εἰκών ἐστιν ἐν Ἀμύκλαις, Σπάρτωνα δὲ Φορωνέως παῖδα θαυμάζοιεν ἂν καὶ ἀρχὴν ἀκούσαντες.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 9.457">Hom. ll. 9.457</bibl>Αἰσχύλος δὲ ὁ Εὐφορίωνος καλεῖ Δία καὶ τὸν ἐν θαλάσσῃ. τρισὶν οὖν ὁρῶντα ἐποίησεν ὀφθαλμοῖς ὅστις δὴ ἦν ὁ ποιήσας, ἅτε ἐν ταῖς τρισὶ ταῖς λεγομέναις λήξεσιν ἄρχοντα τὸν αὐτὸν τοῦτον θεόν.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Unknown</bibl>οὗτος ὁ χρησμὸς δηλοῖ μάλιστα οὐκ ὄντα Ἀσκληπιὸν Ἀρσινόης, ἀλλὰ Ἡσίοδον ἢ τῶν τινα ἐμπεποιηκότων ἐς τὰ Ἡσιόδου τὰ ἔπη συνθέντα ἐς τὴν Μεσσηνίων χάριν.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 4.193">Hom. Il. 4.193</bibl>ὡς ἂν εἰ λέγοι θεοῦ παῖδα ἄνθρωπον.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 2.584">Hom. Il. 2.584</bibl>τοῦτο ᾤκισε μὲν Ἕλιος νεώτατος τῶν Περσέως παίδων, Δωριεῖς δὲ παρεστήσαντο ὕστερον πολιορκίᾳ, καὶ πρῶτοί τε ἐγένοντο οὗτοι Λακεδαιμονίων δοῦλοι τοῦ κοινοῦ καὶ εἵλωτες ἐκλήθησαν πρῶτοι, καθάπερ γε καὶ ἦσαν· τὸ δὲ οἰκετικὸν τὸ ἐπικτηθὲν ὕστερον, Δωριεῖς Μεσσηνίους ὄντας, ὀνομασθῆναι καὶ τούτους ἐξενίκησεν εἵλωτας, καθότι καὶ Ἕλληνας τὸ σύμπαν γένος ἀπὸ τῆς ἐν Θεσσαλίᾳ ποτὲ καλουμένης Ἑλλάδος.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 18.140">Hom. Il. 18.140-141</bibl>καλοῦνται δὲ ἐνταῦθα καὶ πύλαι Καστορίδες, καὶ ἐν τῇ ἀκροπόλει ναὸς καὶ ἄγαλμα Ἀθηνᾶς πεποίηται.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Pindar, Frag. 156(Schroeder)</bibl>ὡς δὲ καὶ Πύρριχος ὄνομα ἦν αὐτῷ, Πινδάρῳ μὲν οὐκ ἔστιν εἰρημένον, λέγουσι δὲ οἱ περὶ τὴν Μαλέαν οἰκοῦντες.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 21.15">Hom. Od. 21.15</bibl>τοῦ γὰρ Ὀρτιλόχου τὸν οἶκον ἐν τῇ Μεσσήνῃ πόλισμα εἴρηκε τὰς Φηράς, καὶ τόδε ἐξηγήσατο αὐτὸς ἐν Πεισιστράτου παρὰ Μενέλαον ἀποδημίᾳ·

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tyrtaeus, unknown location.</bibl>ὁ τοίνυν Ἀριστομένης δόξῃ γε ἐμῇ γέγονεν ἐπὶ τοῦ πολέμου τοῦ ὑστέρου· καὶ τὰ ἐς αὐτόν, ἐπειδὰν ἐς τοῦτο ὁ λόγος ἀφίκηται, τηνικαῦτα ἐπέξειμι.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 2.729">Hom. Il. 2.729</bibl>ἐς τοῦτο τὸ πόλισμα ἀνῳκίζοντο, ἐπεκτείνοντες τὸν ἀρχαῖον περίβολον ἔρυμα εἶναι πᾶσιν αὔταρκες. ἦν δὲ τὸ χωρίον καὶ ἄλλως ἐχυρόν· ἡ γὰρ Ἰθώμη μεγέθει τε οὐδενὸς ἀποδεῖ τῶν ὀρῶν ὁπόσα ἐντός ἐστιν ἰσθμοῦ καὶ δύσβατος κατὰ τοῦτο μάλιστα ἦν.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Tyrtaeus, unknown location.</bibl>ὅτι δὲ καὶ συμπενθεῖν ἔκειτο αὐτοῖς ἀνάγκη, δεδήλωκεν ἐν τῷδε·
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Unknown.</bibl>ἀνεσώσατο δὲ καὶ τὴν ἀσπίδα ἐκείνην, ἔς τε Δελφοὺς
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Rhianus, unknown location.</bibl>χειμῶνας γὰρ καὶ θέρη κατέλεξε, πόας εἰπὼν τὸν χλωρὸν σῖτον ἢ ὀλίγον πρὸ ἀμητοῦ.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Eumelus, unknown location.</bibl>οὐκοῦν ποιῆσαί μοι δοκεῖ τὰ ἔπη καὶ μουσικῆς ἀγῶνα ἐπιστάμενος τιθέντας.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 19.266">Hom. Il. 19.266-268</bibl>οὕτω μὲν τὸ ἀρχαῖον τὰ τοιαῦτα ἐνόμιζον· ἔστι δὲ πρὸ τῶν ποδῶν τοῦ Ὁρκίου πινάκιον χαλκοῦν, ἐπιγέγραπται δὲ ἐλεγεῖα ἐπʼ αὐτοῦ, δεῖμα ἐθέλοντα τοῖς ἐπιορκοῦσι παριστάναι.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 5.544">Hom. Il. 5.544</bibl>καὶ ἐμὲ ἔπειθον λέγοντες· ῥεῖ γὰρ δὴ διὰ τῆς χώρας ταύτης ὁ Ἀλφειός, ἐς δὲ ἄλλην Πύλον οὐκ ἔστιν ἐπενεγκεῖν τὸ ἔπος· Πυλίων γὰρ τῶν ὑπὲρ νήσου τῆς Σφακτηρίας οὐ πέφυκεν ἀρχὴν διοδεύειν τὴν γῆν ὁ Ἀλφειός, οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ ἐν τῇ Ἀρκάδων Πύλον ποτὲ ὀνομασθεῖσαν ἴσμεν πόλιν.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 5.395">Hom. Il. 5.395-397</bibl>εἰ δὲ κατὰ τὴν Ἀγαμέμνονος καὶ Μενελάου στρατείαν ἐπὶ Ἴλιον Ποσειδῶν τῷ Ὁμήρου λόγῳ τοῖς Ἕλλησιν ἐπίκουρος ἦν, οὐκ ἂν ἄπο τοῦ εἰκότος οὐδὲ Ἅιδην εἴη δόξῃ γε τοῦ αὐτοῦ ποιητοῦ Πυλίοις ἀμῦναι. Ἠλεῖοι δʼ οὖν ὡς σφίσι τε εὔνῳ καὶ ἀπεχθανομένῳ πρὸς τὸν Ἡρακλέα ἐποιήσαντο

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 21.446">Hom. Il. 21.446-448</bibl>τὰ μὲν δὴ ἐς τὸ κρανίον τοῦ βοὸς ἐπὶ τοιῷδε ἄν τις εἰκάσειε πεποιῆσθαι· ἔστι δὲ ἐν ὑπαίθρῳ τῆς ἀγορᾶς ἄγαλμά τε Ἀθηνᾶς καὶ πρὸ αὐτοῦ Πατρέως τάφος.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Pamphos, work unknown</bibl>οὕτω διὰ τὴν ἱππικὴν καὶ οὐκ ἀπὸ ἑτέρας προφάσεως τὸ ὄνομα ἔσχηκεν.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 8.203">Hom. Il. 8.203</bibl>δῆλον ὡς γέρα τοῦ Ποσειδῶνος ἐπʼ ἴσης ἔν τε Ἑλίκῃ καὶ ἐν ταῖς Αἰγαῖς ἔχοντος.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 2.573">Hom. Il. 2.573</bibl>Πεισίστρατον δέ, ἡνίκα ἔπη τὰ Ὁμήρου διεσπασμένα τε καὶ
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 5.272">Hom. Od. 5.272</bibl>ἔχοιεν δʼ ἂν καὶ ἄλλως τὸ ὄνομα οἱ ἀστέρες ἐπὶ τιμῇ τῇ Καλλιστοῦς, ἐπεὶ τάφον γε αὐτῆς ἀποφαίνουσιν οἱ Ἀρκάδες.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 15.36">Hom. Il. 15.36-37</bibl>ταῦτα μὲν δὴ ἐποίησεν ὡς ἂν ἰδὼν ἐς τὸ ὕδωρ τῆς Στυγὸς στάζον· βούλεται δὲ καὶ ἐν καταλόγῳ τῶν μετὰ Γουνέως Τιταρησίῳ ποταμῷ ῥεῖν τὸ ὕδωρ ἀπὸ τῆς Στυγός.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Antimachus, unknown location.</bibl>ὁ μὲν δὴ Ὄγκιος Ἀπόλλωνός ἐστι κατὰ τὴν φήμην καὶ ἐν τῇ Θελπουσίᾳ περὶ τὸ χωρίον ἐδυνάστευε τὸ Ὄγκιον, τῇ θεῷ δὲ Ἐρινὺς γέγονεν ἐπίκλησις·
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 23.346">Hom. Il. 23.346</bibl>ἐν δὲ τῇ Θηβαΐδι ὡς Ἄδραστος ἔφευγεν ἐκ Θηβῶν
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Thebaid, unknown location.</bibl>αἰνίσσεσθαι οὖν ἐθέλουσι τὰ ἔπη Ποσειδῶνα Ἀρείονι εἶναι πατέρα, Ἀντίμαχος δὲ παῖδα εἶναι Γῆς φησιν·
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 7.59">Hom. Od. 7.59-60</bibl>ἐθέλουσι δʼ αὐτῷ λαὸς ἐν τοῖς ἔπεσιν ἀνθρώπων οἱ πολλοὶ καλεῖσθαι.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Timotheus, unknown location.</bibl>ἀπεῖδεν ἐς τὸν Φιλοποίμενα τὸ Ἑλληνικὸν καὶ ἐπεσημήναντο τῷ κρότῳ φέρειν ἐς ἐκεῖνον τὸ ᾆσμα. τοιοῦτο ἐς Θεμιστοκλέα ἄλλο ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ πυνθάνομαι συμβῆναι· καὶ γὰρ Θεμιστοκλέους ἐς τιμὴν ἐπανέστη τὸ ἐν Ὀλυμπίᾳ θέατρον.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 11.263">Hom. Od. 11.263</bibl>ὅτι δὲ Ἀμφίων ᾖδε καὶ τὸ τεῖχος ἐξειργάζετο πρὸς τὴν λύραν, οὐδένα ἐποιήσατο λόγον ἐν τοῖς ἔπεσι· δόξαν δὲ ἔσχεν Ἀμφίων ἐπὶ μουσικῇ, τήν τε ἁρμονίαν
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 11.271">Hom. Od. 11.271</bibl>πῶς οὖν ἐποίησαν ἀνάπυστα ἄφαρ, εἰ δὴ τέσσαρες
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 2.498">Hom. Il. 2.498</bibl>χρόνῳ δὲ ὕστερον τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἀρχαῖον ἀνεσώσαντο.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 14.270">Hom. Il. 14.270-6</bibl>τούτου δὲ ἕνεκα ὑπόνοια δὴ παρέστη τισὶν ὡς Χάριτας ἄρα καὶ πρεσβυτέρας οἶδεν ἄλλας Ὅμηρος.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 13.301">Hom. Il. 13.301-2</bibl>Ἐφύρους δὲ ἐνταῦθα ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν τοὺς ἐν τῇ Θεσπρωτίδι ἠπείρῳ λέγει. τὸ μὲν δὴ Φλεγυῶν γένος ἀνέτρεψεν ἐκ βάθρων ὁ θεὸς κεραυνοῖς συνεχέσι καὶ ἰσχυροῖς σεισμοῖς· τοὺς δὲ ὑπολειπομένους νόσος ἐπιπεσοῦσα ἔφθειρε λοιμώδης, ὀλίγοι δὲ καὶ ἐς τὴν Φωκίδα διαφεύγουσιν ἐξ αὐτῶν.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Il. 9.381">Hom. Il. 9.381</bibl>δῆλα δήπουθεν ὡς καὶ τότε προσιόντων τοῖς Ὀρχομενίοις χρημάτων πολλῶν.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">The Great Eoeae, unknown location.</bibl>Ὅμηρος δὲ ἐπιστάμενος ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν Χαιρώνειάν τε ἤδη καὶ Λεβάδειαν καλουμένας, ὅμως τοῖς ἀρχαίοις ἐχρήσατο ὀνόμασιν ἐς αὐτάς, καθότι καὶ Αἴγυπτον τὸν ποταμὸν εἶπεν, οὐ Νεῖλον.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 18.295">Hom. Od. 18.295</bibl>Ἐριφύλην δὲ οὐ χρυσῷ καὶ λίθοις ποικίλον δέξασθαί φησιν ὅρμον. οὕτω τὸ εἰκὸς τῷ σκήπτρῳ πρόσεστιν εἶναι μόνον ποίημα Ἡφαίστου.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 11.577">Hom. Od. 11.577</bibl>οὐκ ἐπὶ μεγέθει πεποιῆσθαι τοῦ Τιτυοῦ φασιν, ἀλλʼ ἔνθα ὁ Τιτυὸς ἐτέθη, Πλέθρα ἐννέα

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <del>Musaeus</del>, Eumolpia</bibl>χρόνῳ δὲ ὕστερον, ὅσον τῇ Γῇ μετῆν, δοθῆναι Θέμιδι ὑπʼ αὐτῆς λέγουσιν, Ἀπόλλωνα δὲ παρὰ Θέμιδος λαβεῖν δωρεάν· Ποσειδῶνι δὲ ἀντὶ τοῦ μαντείου Καλαύρειαν ἀντιδοῦναί φασιν αὐτὸν τὴν πρὸ Τροιζῆνος.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Boeo, work unknown</bibl>ἐπαριθμοῦσα δὲ καὶ ἄλλους τῶν Ὑπερβορέων, ἐπὶ τελευτῇ τοῦ ὕμνου τὸν Ὠλῆνα ὠνόμασεν·
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Boeo, work unknown</bibl>οὐ μέντοι τά γε ἥκοντα ἐς μνήμην ἐς ἄλλον τινά, ἐς δὲ γυναικῶν μαντείαν ἀνήκει μόνων.

<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Pindar, work unknown</bibl>οὗτος μὲν δὴ ταῦτα ἐς μίμησιν ἐμοὶ δοκεῖν τῶν παρʼ Ὁμήρῳ Σειρήνων ἐποίησεν· οὐ μὴν οὐδὲ τρόπον ὅντινα ἀφανισθῆναι συνέπεσε τῷ ναῷ, κατὰ ταὐτὰ εἰρημένα εὕρισκον· καὶ γὰρ ἐς χάσμα γῆς ἐμπεσεῖν αὐτὸν καὶ ὑπὸ πυρὸς τακῆναι λέγουσιν.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0">Minyad, an unknown work.</bibl>ἐπὶ τούτῳ οὖν καὶ Πολύγνωτος γέροντα ἔγραψεν ἤδη τῇ ἡλικίᾳ τὸν Χάρωνα.
<bibl xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="Hom. Od. 11.631">Hom. Od. 11.631 foll.</bibl>πεποίηται δὲ αὐτῷ καὶ ἐν Ἰλιάδι ὁ Νέστωρ ἄλλα τε ἐπὶ Ἀγαμέμνονος καὶ Ἀχιλλέως νουθεσίᾳ καὶ ἔπη τάδε εἰρηκώς·

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse" rend="blockquote"> <label>Speech from Euripides</label> <l met="u">He wins men’s hearts who with a ready hand</l> <l>Confers his favors; he who in the doing</l> <l>Delays and falters is less generous.</l> <l>But I consent to give my child to die</l> <l>For many reasons: first there is no state</l> <l>I count more worthy to accept my gift</l> <l>Than <placeName key="perseus,Athens">Athens</placeName>, peopled by no alien race.</l> <l>For we are of this soil, while other towns,</l> <l>Formed as by hazard in a game of draughts,</l> <l>Take their inhabitants from diverse parts.</l> <l>He who adopts a city, having left</l> <l>Some other town, resembles a bad peg</l> <l>Fixed into wood of better quality,</l> <l>A citizen in name but not in fact.</l> <l>And secondly: it is that we may guard</l> <l>Our country and the altars of the gods</l> <l>That we get children for ourselves at all.</l> <l>This city, though it bears a single name,</l> <l>Holds many people in it. Should I then</l> <l>Destroy all these, when it is in my power</l> <l>To give one girl to die on their behalf?</l> <l>The mere ability to count, and tell</l> <l>The greater from the less, convinces me</l> <l>That this, the ruin of one person’s home,</l> <l>Is of less consequence and brings less grief</l> <l>Than would result if the whole city fell.</l> <l>If I had sons at home instead of girls,</l> <l>When hostile flames beset the city’s walls,</l> <l>Should I not send them forth into the fight,</l> <l>Though fearing for them? May my children then</l> <l>Fight also, vie with men, and not become</l> <l>Mere shapes of vanity within the state.</l> <l>And yet, when mothers send their sons to war</l> <l>With tears, they often daunt them as they leave.</l> <l>I hate the women who above all else</l> <l>Prefer their sons to live and put this thought</l> <l>Before their honor, urging cowardice.</l> <l>But if they fall in battle they obtain</l> <l>A common grave and glory which they share</l> <l>With many others; whereas she, my child,</l> <l>By dying for this city will attain</l> <l>A garland destined solely for herself.</l> <l>And she will save her mother and you too</l> <l>And both her sisters. Is it right to scorn</l> <l>Honors like these? Except in nature’s way</l> <l>This girl whom I shall give for sacrifice</l> <l>To save her native land is not my own.</l> <l>And if the city falls, what further chance</l> <l>Shall I have left me to enjoy my child?</l> <l>So far as rests with me, all shall be saved.</l> <l>Let others rule in <placeName key="perseus,Athens">Athens</placeName>; I will be</l> <l>Her savior, and without my wish no man</l> <l>Shall harm what most concerns our common good,</l> <l>The ancient laws our fathers handed down.</l> <l>Eumolpus and his slavish Thracian train</l> <l>Shall set no trident in our midst or deck</l> <l>It round with garlands, where the olive tree</l> <l>And Gorgon’s golden head have been revered;</l> <l>Nor shall Athena meet with utter scorn.</l> <l>Come, citizens, and use my travail’s fruit</l> <l>To save yourselves and conquer, knowing well</l> <l>That I could never hesitate to save</l> <l>This city for the sake of one poor life.</l> <l>My country, were the love of all your sons</l> <l>As great as mine! You could not suffer ill,</l> <l>And we possessing you would live secure.</l></quote> <bibl>Euripides</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse" rend="blockquote"><l met="u">Nobly comes death to him who in the van</l> <l>Fighting for fatherland has made his stand.</l> <l>Shame and despite attend the coward’s flight,</l> <l>Who, leaving native town and fruitful land,</l> <l>Wanders, a homeless beggar, with his kin,</l> <l>True wife, old father, mother, tender child.</l> <l>Unwelcome will he be where’er he goes,</l> <l>Bowed dawn with hardship and by want defiled.</l> <l>Bringing his house dishonor, he belies</l> <l>His noble mien, a prey to fear and shame.</l> <l>Thus roams the waif unpitied and unloved,</l> <l>He and the line that after bears his name.</l> <l>Be stalwart then. Think not of life or limb;</l> <l>Shielding our land and children let us die.</l> <l>Youths, brave the fight together. Be not first</l> <l>To yield to craven cowardice and fly.</l> <l>Make large your hearts within you. Undismayed</l> <l>Engage in battle with grown men. Be bold;</l> <l>And standing fast forsake not those whose feet</l> <l>No longer keep their swiftness. Guard the old.</l> <l>For shame it is to see an elder fall,</l> <l>Down in the forefront, smitten in the strife,</l> <l>Before the youths, with grey beard, hair grown white,</l> <l>To breathe out in the dust his valiant life,</l> <l>Clasping his bloody groin with clinging hands,</l> <l>(Fit sight indeed to kindle wrath and shame!)</l> <l>His body bared. But those whom youth’s sweet flower</l> <l>Adorns unfaded nothing can defame.</l> <l>Honor of men is theirs, in life, and women’s love;</l> <l>Fair are they too when in the van laid low.</l> <l>Then clench your teeth and, with both feet astride,</l> <l>Firm planted on the ground withstand the foe.</l></quote> <bibl>Tyrtaeus</bibl> </cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse"> <l ana="#met-u">God alone can have this privilege.</l> </quote> <bibl>Simonides Fr. 37.1.14</bibl> </cit>Surely he cannot mean that it is bad to be good, if he proceeds here to say that God alone can have this thing, and attributes this privilege to God only; otherwise Prodicus would call Simonides a rake, and no true Cean.

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse"> <l ana="#met-u">For that man cannot help but be bad</l> <l>Whom irresistible mischance has overthrown.</l> </quote> <bibl>Simonides 37.1.14-16</bibl> </cit> Now who is it that an irresistible mischance overthrows in the command of a ship? Clearly not the ordinary man, for he may be overcome at any time; just as you cannot knock over one who is lying down, but one who is standing; you might knock over a standing man so as to make him lie down,
<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse"> <l ana="#met-u">If he hath fared well, every man is good;</l> <l>Bad, if ill.</l> </quote> <bibl>Simonides Fr. 37.1.17</bibl></cit>

<cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse">Therefore never shall I, in quest of what cannot come to pass, vainly cast my life’s lot upon a hope impracticable—of finding a man wholly blameless amongst us who partake of the fruit of the broad-based earth. <cit xmlns="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0"> <quote type="verse">But I praise and love everyone willingly committing no baseness; for against necessity not even the gods make war.</quote> <bibl>Simonides Fr. 37.1.27ff.</bibl></cit> This also is spoken with the same intent. And then he was stirred to some bitter speech upon men puffed up by fortune. What remains to tell? At last, as I now besought and now threatened, mingling the stern and mild, ‘Had I been Archias,’ he said, ‘I had yielded; but seeing that I am Demosthenes, your pardon, good sir, if my nature recoils from baseness.’
